div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

DEAR NELLTE, I am assu:cd on very -nigh authority that the Most notable change in the latest fashions will be found in the skirts, for rows of gathers appear on many of them at the waist, and consequently the new models fo:m a very striking contrast to those of a few weeks ago, when no skirt was considered up to date unlegs it fitted very closely round the figure below the waist. A charming picture dress in ~the new style which has been bruited to ray notice is made of satin-faced foulard in a rich rose colour, with a white sprigged design on it, and the skirt has four rows of thick cordings all round the bottom. The full bodice has a yoke of finely- tucked white chiffon, with quillings of black and white satin ribbon run on a pleated band of chiffon, and below this there is an accordion-pleated frill of black chiffon, from underneath which appear some pointed pieces of ecru guipure lace: Bands of black lace insertion finish off the sleeves, which have soft puffs of white chitT,on at the wrists, and round the shoulders is worn a white chiffon ruffle, edged with black chenille, and finished off with vety long ends of black chenille, which hang down in front when it is fastened. Some appliquds of Zern lace are sewn on the yoke and collar. A picture hat of Leghorn straw complete this toilette; it is trimmed mind the crown and inside- the brim with insertions of black lace and clusters of shaded pink and red roses, with foliage.

I should like to describe a lovely gown that I saw the other day. It is made of soft white muslin brilliant, mounted on maize-coloured glace silk, and trimmed with transparent insertions of ecru guipure lace. At the bottom of the skirt there areinnumerable little frills, which give a pretty, full effect round the bottom of the feet. The sash is of maize-coloured crepe de Chine, fringed at the ends and fastened with a rosette on the left side. A hat of white crinoline is worn with this, which is trimmed with maize-coloured chiffon and shot blue and green wings, and the parasol is of white chiffon, lined with maize-colour. This model is also vaitable for chiffon or very soft muslins, and could Le made up with an underdress of any colour. Cream-coloured or ecru muslin which is very fashionable just now, may be used instead of white with equally good effect, and a lining of batiste is almost as effective as silk if an inexpensive gown is desired.

Ole sailor-hat appears to be rather in the back- ground at presento except with the very workmanince boating girl, for the picturesque element in dress which is so decided just now obtains on the river as elsewhere. The river hat, above all things, othould be shady, and here, at all events, the toque Is at a discount. One of the smartest hats of the moment, eminently suited to the river, is a coarse burnt straw. trimmed with nothing but a huge careless bow, one or two loops held up with a ()welled pin stuck through.

Elbow-sleeves are again much in vogue, not only for evening gowns, but for those intended for wear at smart garden parties or afternoon concerts. Whey are quite tight-fitting, and are finished by doep frills of lace, longer at the outside than at the inside of the arm. Unlined lace sleeves of this type are seen on both day and evening bodices, hut are met by the long gloves which conceal the rower part of the arm.

For seaside wear there is quite a run on striped Sannels in soft shades of grey, tan, blue and green; blue andgrey, and blue and biscuit being, _perhaps, the two most popular combinations. They are usually made up very simply, with plain skirt and 'reefer coat; but if revers of light blue foulard and small gilt buttons are added, they are decidedly smart-looking when well cut. Striped drill and ique dresses must also be reckoned among those an fashion for holiday wear, but art•linen is more in vogue than either material. This fabric does not lend itself particularly well to the coat-and- skirt style (indeed, a coat of any washing material is rarely a complete success), but looks charming anode up with a full bodice and broad roll collar turned 'back from a, vest of tucked lawn or muslin.

Cirhe most fashionable way of trimming coloured linen govryis—whether, blue, green, tan, or deep- red—is with narrow flat bands of the material, with pipings of white linen on each side. The roll-collar is generally merely edged with a piped band, a foulard tie being knotted under it, but aometimes it has facings of silk or embroidered Sinen. The belt may be of stitched and piped linen, silk, or leather, but it must be either very broad or very narrow, for no " medium-width " belts are permissible this season.
Your loving, JENITIN.

g od boots and gloves. Some women like to be as dressed as possible, and others as undressed as possible for the sea. Toe point to be consi 'ered howcv, r, is combined dece.icy and comfort. Of curse if one's bathing consists of mere bobbing up and down in shallow wa'er one can dross as one likes, and even don smart headeear and corsets, as the Spanioh women used to do at Biarritz. But the majority of us do more than bob up and down in shallow water—and f the n-ire serious buciriess cf swimming, divin floating. etc . the most desirable gown is that built in two parts, the tunic of which frees the neck, whilst the sleevos cover only the tops of the arms. It •cl serge and cashmere are the fabrics and colour most in roqurst. Regarding bathing oaps, the wisest plan Murat to don a white or terra-cotta pure rubber specimen. On the head band of all the newest, little loops appear, and through these a ribbon to match the gown tn, y be passed and arranged in a becoming bow in front. This is by far the simplost and most suc-esful arrangement. The pretty waterproof silk caps shown at outfitters though fascinating to a degree, are really no protection at all from the salt water as many of us have found out to our cost.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

The list of presents bestowed by the Queen after the last performance of " Faust," at Windsor, furnishes evidence that Her Majesty must find these entertain- ments extremely expensive. They represent however, I only one of the calls upon the Queen's private purse,and although there are many wealthier people, yet it is improbable that any of the great millionaires give so much away. The promoters of every charity seek, quite naturally, a subscription from Her Majesty with the invaluable prestige which such sanction affords and one is disposed to regard almost as a curiosity, any object which is not considered to have a claim upon the private purse of the Queen. The Waterloo Chamber in which stage performances and concerts take place at Windsor, is one of the most wonderful apartments in the Castle. Built in com- memoration of Waterloo, of Wellingcon,and the soldiers and statesmen whose names are lieked with tbeee,it has usuallk, little of the theatre about it, but when occ Bioll demands, a stage, also a dais upen which tie green and Royal personages sit, spring up, and the aspect of things is changed. When the brilliant lights flash on the jewels and dresses of the women, and the gorgeous uniforms of the men, the Waterloo Chamber presen s indeed a most magnificent spectacle: Johann Sebastian Bach has been designated" the founder and fatber of German music," and on !he 150th annivelsary of his death, which c ceurred on the 21-t July, the people of Liepzic decided to render somewhat tardy honour to his memory. They have removt d what they believe to be his remains to a vault which has been specially constructed beneath the high altar of the ch arch of St. Thomas. From the contemporariee, Bach obtained but a very small measure of recognition, and he was buried at the Cost of a few shillings in a churchyard, which was subsequently converted into a roadway. The bones taken from the churchyard were et-interred, but with so little care that it is by no means certain which are those ef Bach, although the Leirzic officials examined the question a few years ago, and came to a conclusion which they regarded as satis- factory. As might have been expected, a counterblast has been organised to the "Ladies' League" which Lsdy WFM- borne was mainly instrumental in forming, fer the pro- tection of the froteetant character of the Chinch of England. This society takes the title of "The Church- man's League of Prayer" whose objects are stated to be "to draw together Chuict women in a League of Prayer, during the present attack on Catholic faith and prac- tice." The League also aspires "to unite all who are willing to put Church before party politics and to main- tain the right ef the Church to govern herself in spiritual matters." The last sentence is however, a little ambiguous, as coming from the High Church party, as the whole trouble arises from the unwillingness of the extreme section, to comply with the rulings of the Archbishops and high authorities of the Church. It is moreover clear that the church question will enter lamely into party politic', and it will have a much greater influence at the General Election in England, than many peoplesuppose. Whatever may be said about extending the Parlia- mentary franchise to women, it is generaily conceded that their influence is all to the good in the manaee. ment of local affairs. Few will therefore be disposed to quarrel with the Women's Local Government Societe which has been established to promote the eligibility of women to vote and serve upon the various bo ties in the United Kingdom, which are charged with these dutiea. To a large extent local boards are already thrown open to women voters, but there are still some restrictions which the Society will endeavour to get removed, and also to obtain a lodger and service franchise for wriest,. There is no doubt that the Society is on the winning side, and that the limitation of women's voting rowers, on account of their sex, evil, in due course be removed with regard to the election and constitution of local governing bodies. During the past season of drapers' sales, it cannot hut have struck many of us, yet once again, that all the 1310 St tempting bargains are,generally sneakng, securt d by a rush of people, concerning whom it is safe to Fa 4 that the majority of them never buy ansehine else in the shop until the next sale comes round. The pro- prietors themselves ought to know their own interesta best but stiller it would be an advantage all round, if the first day or two were set aside for regular Cus- tomers. These unfortunate folks are quite out of the running. To push and scramble through hordes of excited women getting one's clothes crumpled and torn often b.yond, recognition, is not a procedure to look forward to with equanimity, and numbers of us shirk it, who would gladly secure a few of the bargains offerred, if this could be accomplished in a little more pleasant manner. The issue of tickets to regular cestemers,and one or two reserved days would be a conside.rable improvement on the present state of affairs. Since the great majority of middle class girls began to earn their own living in the various walks of life now open to them, no one can have failed to have noticed the great irnpreveme, t in their generally nest appearance in dress. It is not so much perhaps that they wear better clothes as it is that they are better selected and cared for, and that after all is the great secret of success and economy in matters of dress. One very important point to the would-be economically clothed, is to remain faithful to one, or at most two colours, and to resist all temptations to ven- ture outside them, or to fritter away money upon chiffons or other perishable items. Further, the neat shirt and sailor hat for every day, wear are wonderful aids to economy. Carefully defined they always lock well, and the money thee enable the wearer to save in more expensive dressmaking and millinery, enables her to spend more upon those two very important items,

div.head: FREE CHURCHES,
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES,
'HARRY LINDSAY."

Mr. IT. Lindsay Hudson ("Harry Lindsayt Of " Methodist Idylls " fame) has been ap- pointed editor of the proposed new Methodist paper, to be called the Methodist Weekly. We understand that the journal is to be published in ::\l'anchester, and that it will devote special attention to the Methodism of the North. Mr. Hudson is already known to a large consti- tuency by his stories. He has accepted his new post with diffidence and hesitation, but he will give the paper of his best, and try to make it a great success.
INTERVIEW WITH THE ItEV. THOMAS LAW.

The Britisl, Weekly of July 19 contained an interesting interview with the Rev. Thomas Law, the Secretary of the National Free Church Council, concerning the Simultaneous Mission, 1991. Mr. Law lays special emphasis on several points. He insists first of all that the mere preparation for the mission will be of untold benefit to all the churches. Again, the mission will lead many ministers to rediscover the missioner within themselves. That is, they will discover that they have the faculty, and that upon them is laid the duty of making direct appeals to their hearers to accept Christ as their Lord and Master and Saviour. The local Councils are taking up the proposal with enthusiasm, and the Central Office is up to the neck in the preparatory and organising work.

div.head: RESULTS OF THE MISSION.
div.p: THE RESULTS OF THE MISSION.

With regard to the results, Mr. Law re- marked: "No, I'm not going to make an esti- mate in figures. Mr. Parr mentioned one hundred thousand at Sheffield Mr. Bourne does not see why London alone should not yield one million new members to the churches; and Mr. Hughes speaks of three million or four million as the total result. But it is not a question of arithmetic at all. It is the question of the duty of the churches to the great out- side masses. The moral and religious condition of the country, and especially of the large towns and cities, loudly calls for evangelistic effort on a far larger scale than has hitherto been attempted."
HOW not TO PROMOTE CHRISTIAN UNION.

The Bishop of Truro, addressing the Home Reunion Society, told a tale to illustrate the struggles of a dying Nonconformity! He said that he had recently been told by clergy of cases in which seven candidates for Confirma- tion had been told they would be turned out of doors if they were confirmed. The Bishop has been invited to produce the evidence or authority upon which he made his statement, but he has said in reply nothing that he will give permission to 'oe published. It is surely fair comment to say that if the Bishop cannot give Nonconformists an opnortu nity of investigating cruel charges of this sort, he should not have made them. Home reunion will certainly not be promoted by flinging out loose and unsup- ported accusations against Free Churchmen.
THE CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR WORLD'S
CONVENTION.

This great international gathering, held in London, has undoubtedly been a conspicuous success, as far at least as success can be judged by attendance. The Rev. C. M. Sheldon, the author of "In His Steps," was perhaps the most drawing arne on the programme. Mr. Sheldon is no orator, and many people were deeply dis- appointed by his speeches. For an hour, during each day of the Convention, Mr. Sheldon allowed himself to be bombarded with questions, but these dealt mainly with the work of the Societies, and were not of general interest. During his visit to London Mr. Shel- don has been besieged by throngs of people seeking his autograph. With re- markable patience and good humour he sought at first to satisfy the demands of his admirers, but he was obliged to give way and stop the practice.

div.head: REV. W. CUFF.
div.p: THE REV. W. CUFF.

The Rev. W. Cuff, the President ot the Baptist Union, has broken down under the heavy burden of his work. Mr. Cuff has been toiling tremendously for the Baptist Twentieth Century Fund, and he has sent a pressing appeal to his friends not to let the Fund suffer on account of his illness. Mr. Cuff has gone to Norway to gather strength, and we trust that the autumn will find him back at his work in renewed vigour.

div.head: REV. MARSHALL MATHER.
div.p: THE REV. MARSHALL MATHER.

• The only thing that marred the annual assembly in Manchester of the United Methodist Free Churches was the absence, through prolonged illness, of the minister of the church in which the Assembly met—the Rev. Marshall Mather. Mr. Mather has been away for many weeks, and the earlier time suggested for his return by his medical advisers was August or September. Mr. Mather is benefit._ ing by the complete rest and change, but the recovery of strength is slow, and the time originally fixed for his return to duty will pro- bably hare to be extended a little. Mr. Mather is well known outside his own connexion as a very clever writer of Lancashire idylls.

div.head: CRUEL WE,ONG TO NONCONFORMISTS.
div.p: A CRUEL WE,ONG TO NONCONFORMISTS.

The Rev. J. R. Cooper, Secretary of the Helston Free Church Council, writes to the Free Church Chrontcle to state two cases of Anglican persecution that came under his notice as Pastor or both Holston and Hayle Baptist Churches: A young lady, a teacher in a National day-school, was led to seek member- ship with the Baptist Church. She made known her intention to the Canon, who spoke to her and gave her a pamphlet, telling her if she persisted in her determination, she must leave the school. Her father a2so said if she lost her situation she must leave her home. She could do no other than fulfil what she believed to be the will of her Lord, and was dismissel with a month's pay instead of notice. A scholar in Mr. Cooper's Sunday- school had to forsake both school and church in order to become a pupil-teacher in the National School at Holston.

div.head: TROUBLES IN CHINA.
div.p: THE TROUBLES IN CHINA.

Among the victims of the reported Pekin mas- sacre are missionaries of the London Missionary Society and of the Church of England. There are many missionan.es throughout the Chinese Empire who at tin.; moment stand in great peril. The Arch bishop of Canterbury, speak- ing at the Mansion House, London, struck the right note in his reference to the thrilling events that are taking place in the Far East: "A great many of the missionaries," said Dr. Temple," instead of being daunted by the fact that they are in danger, are inspired by the prospect of martyrdom in the Berme of their Lord. It will be found to be as it has been from the beginning, that the blood of the martyrs has been the seed of the Church.

div.head: TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
div.p: THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
BY JOSEPH HOCKING,
Authc,r of "The Birthright," "Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," ecc.

div.head: CHAPTER XIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XIII.
THE BEGINNING OF TIIE STRUGGLE.

Alizon Neville looked forward with interest towards Duncan Rutland's visit to the Priory on the following Wednesday. The Christmas and New Year's feF;tivities had long corde to an end, and :Lady Neville had pcstponed going to London for a few weeks, in order to fall in with Father Ritzoom's plans. For although her ladyship generally went to town for the season, she was by no means a society woman. Neither did Alizon care much for the ordinary round of London festivities. Hers was an intellectual, rather than a pleasure loving nature, and while by no means a pedant, she was fond of conversing with cultured people. Her hie was rather quiet at the Priory, and so she welcomed the thought of meeting with Rutland, and of hearing him talk. She was much interested in the Jesuit's scheme for the conversion of Rutland, but her faith in it was not strong. Had she known the whole of his plans she would doubtless have felt differently, in all probability she would have refused to participate in it. Like all true Catholics, however, she believed that such as he remained Protestant because of prejudice, and because of ignorance concerning the great truths of her faith. And yet, as she remembered how he had torn Father Sheen's argu- ments to pieces, she doubted whether being brought into close contact with Catholics at the Priory would effect the desired change. True she had great faith in the influence of her mother, while Father Ritzoom almost awed her. His strong face and unfathomable eyes led her to believe that he had entered into the secrets of power, and was thus enabled to achieve what to others would be impossible. During the morning her mother had handed her a letter from Father Sheen, and when she had read it, a look of satisfaction came into her eyes. "You see we shall not have his help in entertain- ing Mr. Rutland," remarked Lady Neville. "I see," she replied. "He has gone to Manchester to meet Father Ritzcom, he says. I thought the Jesuit was to stay in Lynford for some time."

"I thought so too; but it seems that he has been called to Manchester. I suppose he goes to Ireland to-morrow, and then he will come back here in about a fortnight. I have invited him to stay at the Priory. Ile is a wonderful man." "I am almost afraid of him," said the girl. "Are you? Doubtless ho is very clever, and is of immense power in the Church. I suppose he has great. influence in Rome." "1-1-e seems to know everyone, too," said the girl. "By the way, what shall we do to entertain Mr. Rutland when he comes ? "
"Well, we must shew him round the house, and then, perhaps, you can play billiards with him until dinner."

"But supposing he can't play? " "It doesn't matter. His interests are so varied that it will be easy to amuse him." When Duncan reached the Priory he was received with a welcome smile, so gracious, indeed, was Lady Neville, that the young man remembered the advice of the old weaver, and wondered if it was of value. He dismissed it in a moment, however. He remembered that he was dealing with a woman who, whatever her religious prejudices might be, would scorn to do an unworthy act. He did iv,t seem at all chagrined at Father Sheen's non-appearance, indeed, the afternoon passed like a pleasant dream. Both Alizon and Lady Neville accompanied him in his tour through the rooms, and the young man was charmed. Old rooms, old pictures, old curiosities, delighted him beyond measure; he listened with intense interest to the descriptions given of events of bygone days, and in spite of his beliefs, could not help sympathis- ing with the men who in the reign of Elizabeth had been secreted in the Priory by the old Nevilles who had been true to their faith, rather than to the laws of their country. And yet no word was uttered about religion. Even when they visited the private chapel, and both Alizon and Lady Neville genuflected before the altar, no word was uttered; they performed their act of homage reverently but naturally, neither did they pay any seeming atten- tion to the attitude of the young Protestant. This visit was the forerunner of others. They did not happen very often, because a large and growing chur h took up a great deal of his time. Still he found his way to the Priory as often as he could, and each visit deepened the impression which the first had made. The atmosphere of this old home was so different from that of the other houses which he visited. Everything was so quiet, so orderly, so pure. He could not help comparing the conversation of Lady Neville and Alizon with that of his church officers. These men were kind and cordial, but in some of them was a taint of coarseness. They laughed at jokes which he did not like, and they did not care for some of the things which he loved. Besides, a minister's life is not a bed of roses. None but those who have had the care of a church can know of the thousand things which happen to wound a sensitive nature. The excitement of the debate was over, end things had settled down to their normal state. The people were proud that their minister had borne himself so valiantly, but they held that he had only done his duty, and so no more need be said about the matter. Some few men who longed for publicity wrote letters to the Lynford Observer, but they were read by only very few, and with languid interest. The congregations at Tudor continued to be very large, and the increased activities of the church caused the minister a greatly added amount of work.

People with but few interests naturally live in a very narrow world, and as a consequence, grow jealous, and often fault-finding. They magnify their own importance, and feel hurt if others do not realise it. Duncan found this to his cost. Such conversations as the following were often taking place, and each one of them wounded the young man, sorely. "Sono, Mester Duncan." "Oh, Mrs. Bray, how are you to-day?" "Only middlin . Avv noaticed as aa tha wart baan to gi' me the goa-by, so aw jist spok. Aw've bin very poorly. Yo' eerd on, aw spoase ?" "No, I hadn't heard." "Yi, but I 'ave. Why, I've noo.n been i'side Tudor for three week. Ain't yo' noa.ticed? " ; "No, I hadn't noticed." ' "Yi, aw thowt as much. That's all th noatice yo' tak' ov foak been away fro' chapel." "Well, you see it's difficult to notice in a large congregation who's present and who isn't." "Yi, aw spoase so. ...A.w'm one o' th' poor people, and so no noatice is took ov me. I 'eerd as aa yo' were in ear street; yo' called to see Mrs. Brown and Mrs. Longley, but yo' noan corned to see me. Yi, but yore norm like owd Mester Simpson when oo win- minister at Tudor, 'OO never neglected me. Good tuornin', Mester Duncan." 'lbis may seem but a matter of little importance, but such conversations made Pinican miserable for days. He did all the visiting he was able; but the church and congregation were large, and lived all over the town, and thus a great deal of time was taken up in visiting a few people. It took him a long time, moreover, to know the members of his flock, and the history of the various families became confused in his mini. If he called at a housz-, however, and confessed his ignorance concerning any member of the family, it was often taken as an offence. In short. he soon discovered that try as hard as he might, there were a number of people who v.rwoble7l at him, and spoke as if he neglected his ,Aork. • This fact came to him in various ways, and he w,3.8 quick to inter- pret the hints which fell. In fact, the minister does not exist who pleases everybody, and as men grow older they cease to expect it, but Duncan was young and sensitive, and so every approach to fault-finding hurt him more than some direct attack would hurt many others. True he found joy in his work, a joy unspeak- able. He loved preaching, loved to prepare for his pulpit work, and his heart rejoiced beyond measure as he saw that young men and women were being influenced by his work. On the other hand, he found no pleasure in many of the meetings he wan called upon to attend. Committee meetings, mothers' meetings, sewing meetings, and a host of others, were to him weariness of the flesh. And yet he was expected to attend them, and if he didn't, the fact was hinted to him in some form or another. One society grumbled that he took no interest in its welfare, and another complained that Its meetings never made any headway since the lad minister left them. I lie dimovqrod too, that although this Church WO

supposed to be free, it was bound by rules formu- lated a century ago, and often when he advanced something which he thought good for the working of the Church, he would be immediately met with a question as to what Rule 45 said about the matter. Of course the great rrass of the people was with him, and realised that never since the Church was formed had it been such a power for good, but many grumbled at innovations, and some would rather that the work should be at a standstill, than done in any other way than their own. And so it came about that one jealous man stung him on the one side, and some conceited lad pricked him on the other, and he, because he was of a highly- wrought nature, felt pained beyond measure. At some of the meetings he attended, men, who knew no more of theology than of Sanscrit, aired their opinions with great confidence ; while the lads who hardly knew the A.B.C. of thinking, told him what he ought to do. He remembered the position held by the vicar, of the parish in which Tudor was situated, and sighed. Bonietimes when he was in a despondent mood, he wondered whether such methods of Church government were not contrary to the best interests of religion, and asked himself whether a minister could exercise a truly legitimate influem e while I:e was regarded by the Church as en ply a layman, with no more authority than themselves.

He reflected that he had spent six yearn of his lire in stlidying the vital questions of church and religious life, and yet some weaver, or clogger, with the assurance of ignorance, treated his words as of the same value as his own.

Thus it came about that his visits to the Priory became trebly a pleasure to him. Here he met with people who understood him, people who were cultured, who read the b( oks he loved, and who enjoyed the thoughts that to him made life worth the living. Several weeks bad passepince the debate, and Spring was fast approaching, the wide stretches of moors became less and less dreary, while, in spite of the smoke, the grass became greener, and the green leaves began to appear. Duncan had seen Father Sheen twice since the meeting to consider cab shelters, and on each occasion the old priest had been very cordial. He had been to the Priory four times, and on each occasion the influence of its inmates became greater. Indeed, it became his delight to go to the old house, and thus when, one day, a letter from Lady Neville reached him, asking him to meet Father Ritzoom, a renowned scholar, who had brought with him some curious ancient manuscripts, he accepted the invitation with eagerness, and looked forward to conversation with a man who was a scholar and a thinker.
CHAPTER XIV.
ROW DUNCAN RUTLAND'S EYES WERE OPENED,

Duncan Rutland was much impressed by the learning, as well as by the geniality of Father Ritzoom. The manuscripts mentioned by Lady Neville proved to be some old parchments which had been recently discovered in one of the ancient monasteries in Palestine. They were said to be copies of parts of the Epistles, and were of great value in proving both the genuineness and authen- ticity of those Epistles. Duncan, who was a very fair Latin scholar, entered eagerly into a debate with Father Ritzoom concerning their authorship, %nd presently the priest gave him a very interesting account of the incidents which led to their dis-

covery. It appeared that an old man living in the monastery gave up his whole time to decipher- ing and translating the various versions of the New Testament; dealing with the Epistles which Protestants declared to be uncanonical, 'as well as those which they had accepted. While busily searching among the vast collection of papers which were contained in the convent library, he discovered a crypt, and on further investigation, unearthed the precious writings on parchment which they were that night examining. "Those old monasteries must be splendid store- houses of rare lore," remarked Duncan presently. "Yes," repiied Ritzoom, "and the Church has ever been careful to treasure such riches. Through- out all the ages, even those when the clouds have been hanging heavily, she has always set aside her scholars to investigate, and thus to know the value of her great inheritance." "Yes," replied Duncan, "and your position as the oldest Church has enabled you to have the greatest possible advantage in this direction." "Naturally; no other section of the community can have access to our treasures," replied the priest, "that is, without our consent. The Greek Church has never been in a position to obtain these valu- able relics of the past, while as for the Protestants --well, they are but of yesterday." "That is true," remarked Duncan, thoughtfully. "Of course, went on the priest, "we have had to be careful of such MSS., it would have been a sin to have cast our pearls before swine. They have had to be guarded by the wise men in all ages. Had they been given to the ignorant, the thoughtless, the greatest riches of the Church would either have been destroyed, or turned to wrong uses. It would have been like giving ignorant quacks liberty to dabble with the mysteries of medicine." "You do not believe in the old adage, Vox populi, vox Dei " said Rutland. believe it to be a device of the devil," replied the priest. "Why, just fancy the danger accruing from such a system. Think of placing power in the hands of the vulgar crowd. Supposing you gave over the government of your country to the mob; think of the anarchy which would result." "And yet in a sense it is in the hands of the snob," remarked' Rutland. "In a sense! But what sense? This so-called enfranchisement of the people is only a plaything to appease the cravings of ignorant children. As a matter of fact, the government of England is in the hands of the few. The Prime Minister of the country, or the few who may be in league with him, formulate the measures which shall be brought before the House of Commons, which is itself only a debating society. In the end the members vote for the thing their leaders advocate." "That is true in part, but only in part." "A very grist part. Why, how much do you or I know of what goes on in the Cabinet P I read , the Times religiously every day; but I am in entire ignorance of what goes on in the councils of those who rule the land. Some time ago there were great naval preparations at Plymouth and elsewhere, there was much talk about the mobilisation of the British forces. I asked various members of Parlia- ment belonging to the Government what was the meaning of it, and they were as ignorant as I was. Shortly after the Prime Minister spoke at a repre- sentative gathering, but he coolly told his hearers that he did not feel disposed to tell what it meant. Then we talk about the enlightenment of the British public." "True again," said Rutland, "but, then, if a Government does not please the people, that Government is turned out at the next election." "Yes, and another takes its place, which acts in entirely the same way. Of course, it sometimes appears as though the people rule: but they do not. It is the few Ivho rule, and not the many. The newspapers raise a great hue and cry, and the people howl, but what effect has it?" and the priest laughed quietly. "Mark you, I do not object to this," went on Ritzoom, "rather, I be- lieve in it. A mob should never govern, a mob should have all its thinking done for it. This is true in all realms of life, it is the few who should tontrol, and who, as a matter of fact, do control. "Yes," replied Duncan, "but it is also true that these cliques have sown the seeds of revolution; they have legislated for their 'own class, they have kept. all the power to themselves, with the result that the poor people have been oppressed and down-trodden, and the natural outcome of oppres- sion is vice and ignorance." "There you mistake me," replied the priest. "1 'believe that the heads of any community should regard themselves as the protectors of the common people. They should treat them as a father treats his children. He should do the very best for their comfort and their happiness, but directly he gives them the government of a household, anarchy, misery follows. This is true in relation to the placing of such valuable documents as this in the hands of the ignorant," and he pointed to the MSS. they had been discussing. "It can be dealt with only by students, by scholars, by those who know the value of such things. It is only scholars who can translate, it is only scholars who can teach the crowd the truths that they contain." Duncan saw the drift of what the priest was saying; it was really an attack on the position he bad taken when he gave his lecture on the "Right of Private Judgment." He saw, moreover, thar the Jesuit's words were full of fallacy, but at that moment the way to answer him did not appear. For one thing, he was influenced by the strong personality of the priest, he exercised a kind of charm which made his words seem weightier than they ought, and for another, he realised that he was the guest of Lady Neville, and that both she and Alison were listening carefully to every word that was said.

•..ror my own par! , e I:t,r agree mit,* you," said Lady Neville pre,eutiy. "In soma respects lam a Socialist, that is, 1 believe-that a fair chance should be giien to all. If there is 2 man in the mob who has intelligence, and who longs for culture, then by all means give him that culture."

"Your ladyship can have no more ardent sup- porter than I," remarked Ritzoom, blandly. "in that sense our Church is the greatest socialistic, force in the world. Is it not a fact that through all the ages our priesthood, our scholars, have come largely from the common people? In every town, in every village we have recognised genius, aye, anything of more than ordinary ability, where ever -we have seen it, and that genius, however poor, has been given his chance. As you know, your ladyship, there have been Popes since St. Peter whose calling has been no higher than he upon whom the Church was built. But that is scarcely my contention. What I maintain is that the government of all communities should be given to the wise and that the ignorant should not deal with those things for which they are utterly unfitted."
"I propose we have some singing," said Ritzoom presently. "Come, Miss Alizon, I am sure you will not refuse us."

Without a word the girl went to the piano and commenced singing. Duncan had never heard her before; indeed, he did not know that she possessed any gifts in this direction, he was therefore sur- prised at the brilliance of her performance. She had a rich contralto voice, and sang with great sweetness and power. She chose some of the old Catholic Passion music, and rendered some of the solos in such a way that Rutland's heart was stirred to the depths. As he sat listening he forgot all that the priest had said, and for the time became almost oblivious to his surroundings. It seemed as if he were in some old Cathedral, and that the whole a,mosnhere of the place was pure and uplifting; ho felt as the old patriarch must, have felt when he heard the words: "Take off thy shoes from cif thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Outside the wind made music among the trees, but no other sound disturbed the silence of the night, while within the old Priory walls the girl poured out her soul in the music of those who had entered that sanctuary which may not be defamed by the unworthy. Rutland listened like one entranced. Through- out the day his feelings had been wounded by people who were kind, but who did not understand his sensitive nature, ho' to-night everything tended to soothe, to heal. Father Ritzoom had appealed to the intellectual side of his life, while now this beautiful girl ministered to his deeper feelings. The words she sung seemed to be a prayer for him, and somehow life became sweeter, holier, as he listened. What if her faith differed from his? What though she regarded him as an heretic? They were both as one in the great prayer she breathed forth in song. Why should he repudiate those who professed the Catholic faith? Did we not owe to them some of the divinest music the world had 'ever heard? The Church which had nurtured those souls who had entered so deeply into the spirit of harmony could not he base. Besides, he had always admitted that Catholicism had given to the world the purest of saints. And so he became swayed by the music as tree-tops are swayed by the passing breeze. , About nine o'clock in the evening another visitor was announced. This. proved to be a young maft who lived about five miles away, and who was the only son of a Catholic squire. He was warn3lY welcomed by both Lady Neville and Alizon, while Father Sheen seemed to regard him as an old friend. When he was introduced to Father Ritzoom; the stranger professed great delight at seeing him, but he was cold and distant to Rutland.

it seemed that he had come to the Priory crt horseback, in order to bring a message from hit father, and Duncan was not long before he noticed the esprit de corps which evidently existed between the old Catholic families. The affectionate respect with which he treated Father Sheen also struck him. It was so different from the way in which the members of his own church regarded him. he knew that he was the target for every critical shaft which the discontented members of his congrega" tion might see fit to send forth, while this priest commanded the respect of all. Before long Duncan had the impression that Lady Neville was anxious for him to go. He sof. that young Arthur Stanley had some news whitc; he wished to communicate, and so soon after

young squire's arrival he rose to go. "And I will walk back with you," said Father, Sheen. "Ritzoom, I hope you will not be troubled. by the Priory ghost." "Nothing troubles me," replied the Jesuit.. "I've seen too many strange things to be troulo7 by what Lancashire folks call a boggart ' P ' • s. I'll call and see you to-morrow so that you may be' fully informed." A few minutes later Duncan and the old priett were walking towards Lynford. "It's been a delightful evening," said the young man. . _

"Yes," replied the other; "her ladyship 15 ti model hostess, and Ritzoom is one of the most entertaining fellows I know. You don't bloc Mr. Arthur Stanley, I think ? " "No, I never met him until to-night." "He belongs to a very old family, almost as old as the Nevilles. He will be wealthy some dal, too. I suppose he is an aspirant for Miss Alizon's hand." "Indeed!" "Yes. I should not be surprised if he had not come on that errand. I think it would be la delightful arrangement. The estates of the two families join, and he is really a most estimable fellow. I thought she greeted him very kindly to- night, didn't you?" "I really did not pay much attention." "Oh, but she did. He has been in love with her for years. I must say it would give me joy to celebrate the marriage sacrament. She is a beauti- ful girl, and as good as she is beautiful. Arthur Stanley will be a lucky fellow if he gets her. Don't you think so ? " "She is very charming," replied Duncan, e'ricl the priest noticed that his voice sounded strangely husky. "Is Father Ritzoom staying at the Priori long?" asked Rutland, presently. "About a month, I think. It is possible he will arrange for a Retreat there."

"A.Retreat ? " "Yes. I suppose you scarcely know the meaning of the term. ' • "No; but I think I can guess what you mean. "Very likely. It is simply a means for devout Catholics to deepen their spiritual life. Put in plain words, a number of people will for a fer days leave the excitements of the world for the purpose of prayer. Father Ititzoom will be the officiating priest. I suppose you would not care to attend?"

"I—l don't know. I think not." "Oh, these Retreats are blessed occasions of grace. They make the spiritual world a greater reality. We all need them. But here I am sV home. Good-night." The young man hurried on like one demented.. When he reached his lodgings he threw himself is the armchair before the fire. Every member of the household was in bed, and so perfect stillness reigned. The fire burnt lower and lower, and the air grog cold; but he sat still. Midnight struck, but be never moved a muscle. His face was as pale al that of a corpse, his features were as still as thoe• of a statue. Presently he heard a step in the street outside. It was simply a policeman on his beat, but the sound disturbed him. He sat up and stared around the room like one dazed. "Great Heavens!" he cried, hoarsely. gct cannot bear it, no I cannot bear it!" The first part of the Jesuit's prophecy bad beel fulfilled. Duncan Rutland realised that he love" Alizon Neville with all the strength of his nature-
(To be continued.)

div.head: WARRINGTON CONSERVATISM.
div.p: WARRINGTON CON- SERVATISM.
Opening of a New Club in Orford-lane. Lord Newton and the General Election.

An irnpoitaet event in connection with local Coneerva- tism teok place on Saturday atternoon, when Sir Peter Carlene Walker, Bart., formally opened the new club premises of the Warrington Junior Censervative Associa- tion in Orford-lane. The building was very many years ago the residence of the late Mr. John Rylands. It hits been transformed into a comfortable club, containing billiard reams, card rooms. See., and there is also a bowling green attached to it. Charming weather favoured the opening ceremony which was performed in the presence of a large number of notabilities. Among those present were Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. (who presided), Lord Newton. Sir Peter Carlaw Walker, Mr Robert Pierpoint, M.P., Colonel Richard Pilkington, M.P , for the Newton Division, Messrs J C Parr, Henry Greenall, J Menne, John White, Cyril Greenall, John Fairclough, and J E Seeker ; Aldermen Feirclough,Suttou,Francomb,and Hietchinsou; Councillors Baird, Bennett, Greening, A Jolley, W J Forshaw, Lee, John Roberts. and Scnettiurst,Dr Fox,and Messrs E Draper, W H J Jerkin', L Voisey, C S Burgess Thomas Mason, W L Williams, E J Hall, R Chadwick. .1 Fulton Smith, J H Smethurst, G Mather. W James, P Wright, E Ellis, A J Sharp, D Smith, T C Brooke, G E Turley, C Plunkett, George Waekine, H Fairclough Charles Hoe ind, T H Ashcroft, E Aukiand, William Holbrootc, Herhert Haves (maualer of the club), R Isherwood, John Taylor, J Bettersby, James Newton, James Rnbinson, J Hambe, J H G Hammen, F H Autiland, C R Burton, J Peers, Peter Wells, P Edgar, P Randall, TPe icc.ck, and John Hughes. Orford-lane was gaily decorated with flags and bunting and maey of the inhabitants watceed the arrival of the visitors. Mr. W. L. WILLIAM 4 seconded the vote of thanks. He said the opening of the new clue marked an important epoch in the political history of Warrineton, and he was sure Sir Peter Walker's presence that clay would stimu- late the members of the Junior Conservative Associa- tien to further and renewed (f f )rti en behalf of th C in- .iervative cause in the town. (Applause). Reviewing the brier history of junior Conservatism he saio it was first brought into existence on J.nuary 25th, 1898, and from the commencement had the encyarag •metil of the leaders of the party, and in particular their friends Mr J. C. Parr, Mr John White, Alderman Sutton, Council- lors Bennett, Greening, Roberts, and numerous others. On many occasions he (the speaker) and various other members of the Association had formed ds putati ins to wait upon Mr. Wbit +, Mr. H .nry Greenall, Mr. Parr, Mr. Pierpoint and ot wr leaders of tee party, and they had impressed upon them the desirability of having a club Iks this so thet they could stimu'ate the young blood in the veins of weak Conser- vative young men. He was pleased to say teat day they had achieved what had long been their ambition, and it was principally due to the assistance they had received from the leaders of the party. (Applause). One fact that they possessed such a building for their club was owing to the liberality of Sir Peter Welker. (Applause). He (the speaker) trusted the members would use it as ii it were their own bones, and that they would often meet there to discuss political matter'. (Hear, hear). Though they possessed such a club they would not be carried away by its social environment. but would be stimulated to renewed exertions n benalf of the cause. (Applause.) The motion on bein, put to the meetine was carried with acclamation and cseers were given fir Sir Peter and Lady Walker ancaup-n a suggestion from one of the audience, for the baby. Sir PETER WALKER in reply said that anything he could do for the Conservative cause and anything he could do for the town of Warrington be would willing in. (Applause.) He had worke 1 in Warrington some five and twenty years ago and had worn the good old Lancashire clog. (Laughter and applause.) He 54w that the bowling green attached t the club was not in good condition, and if they would allow him he would have it laid and put out in the best way it could pip- sibly be done. (App! else.) He thanked them on behalf of himself, his wife, and the Labs,. (Laughter and cheers). Lord NEWTON, who was cordially received, referred to the general election. The great q iestion which everyone w•ts asknoe, themselves, paaricularly his tw Itenourable friends Mr. Pinpoint and Colonel Pilkioeton, was when was that eventful d.y going to arrive Mien was the general election which they hoard so much about going to take place. He considered he had got a very sound personal opinion mem the General Election. He thought there was no reason whatever why an elec- tion should not take place because it happened to be inconvenient to their pceitical opponents. He could net see any reason why they should consult the feelings, wishes, or inclinations of their opponents in any respect whatever ; the persons whose convenience ought to he eensulted were their own supporters and friends. (Hear, hear.) When he saw their opponents, united for ono-- which was an extremely rare spectacle—(laughter)— ersing out with one voice that a General Election at the present moment weu'd be a meet indefensible proceed- ing, he was inclined to think that this was the very moment to cheese for the election. (Laughter.) And he tnnught it highly probable that his two Perliamentary friends would be disposed to aeree with him. ("I think se.") Besides it was always better to get a disagreeable thing over, and he did not Iteow of any more disagree- able thing than a General Election. The great question was, would a General Election be beneficial to the c untry or not? He suppossd that views on that point were divided. There was a great deal to be said on both sides, but there was nothing to be said in favour of the views of the Radical party, tile people who for years had bet n dinning in their ears that they ought to have an election every five years and if possible he was not sore whe her they had reduced the p nod to two years or one year. What would he the case if an election were to take place now? H. had no doubt that Mr. Pierpeint and Cnlouel Piikingten would be returned without opposition and that the same Sort of thing would happen over a large part of the country. Let them consider what this would mean. They had had exnerience during the past Parliament of the extremely unsatisfactory nature of a small and weak Opposition. If there was an election now almost every- body wnu'd be bound to vote for Conservative or Unionist candidates, because in all probability pe .ple won dbe voting upon the Tranevaal war arad nothing else. The Conservatives and Unionist party would be returned by an enormous usajority,and then doubtless a reaction would set in. People wool 1 begin to feel the eff eta of this war, which was not even yet at an end. Toe+, would begin to feel the 'xis once of the other burdens which would be laid upon them in connection with the war, and no doubt: their dissatisfaction at having to pay increased taxes would lead to their showing a want of gratitude for what they had received from Conservative and Unionist Governments in the past. A steady leakage would set in, and the enormous majority would in time to a great extent melt away. This was one of the objections to having an eleclen now But the matter must, after all, be left in the hands of the Cabinet, with whom alone the decision could rest. Whenever the election came he hoped that intelligent electors would not vote simply on the one questien whicti happened to be uppermest, but would take :a patriotic view of the responsibilities of this country. We were not at the end of our difficulties in South Africa. We had had to make vast sacrifie-s, and there would, unfortunately, be nothing correep onding to them in the shnce of results. That, however, was not the fault of the Gevernment, who had been driven into the war by the deliberate action cf Mr. K tiger and his friends. It would have been as impossible for a Rid:cal as it was for a Conservat lye Government Co have resisted this war. and this was a fact which must be borne in mind. But the Transvaal war was not the only- thing that the country ought to consider when an election came. He could not remember a time when the country stood in a more critical condition than at the present momenTM. In common with the rest of Europe we had been surprised by one of the mest horrible and dreadful tragedi.s of modern times, the massacre of our represen- tatives and the European communities in China. It was one of the most horrible and surprising things that had ever happened in history. All the nations which con- sidered themselves most civiized had been deliberating and disputing amenest themselves as to which por'l ms of China they should take, and in the mean- while, under their very noses, the C'n'inese "had been deliberately preparing for the expulsion of Europeans. This was a fact which would lead to great complications in the future It was not necessary to he mush of a prophet to see that Europe had a very grave and serere task in hand, that the difficulty would not consist solely in avenging the massacres which had taken place, but that difficulties were bound to arise b tween the Various European nations who had interest in the Far East. This was Only one of the problems that would c mfront them when they had to vote at the General Election, but with the tlermometer in its pre- sent state he did not wish to indulge in the considera- tion o' any further problems. (14 iughter). Ho afire] them to vote as they voted before, anti be was sure that any man who recorded his vote for Mr. Pierpoint would be able- to look upon the action with a clear conscience. (Applause.) Colonel PILKINGTOIS. M.P., &livered a brief address. Be was of mondial that during the time the Unionist Government bad been in power it had male no great rrestatte. If there had been mistakes they had been of a small and unimportant character. The great steps of policy by which they had cemented the empire,by which they hal raised the enthusi ism and the patriotism ot the reoplP from the centre to the extreme end of the , colonies, every step which had been taken had bean of a wise, warm, and patriotic character. In Esypte and South Africa the policy had always been strong, careful, wise and far-seeing, and especially with regard to Africa the Government did their work up to the hilt, and if more money wa.s wanted it would be found because they were rl(termire i to make a good job ot everything they undertet k. (Hear, hear, and applause.) With re- gard to the next General Election, he did not care inueh when it came—be 'ironer the better—but if it was nut off it wruld he all the same to him. (Lauehtss.) W:th • regard to affairs in China and other important events now taking place, all he had to say to them was Sand to Parliament a united party to de the country's work as it ought to be done. We can &al with the Chinese question and we shall be able to do so it you will return a strong and united body of men to Parliament to enable tbsen to continue the same wise and able policy." (Appl+uee.; So far as tae General Election was con- cerned, he had no doubt that Warrington and Newton would be ready and willing to do theirduty,aad so would Lancashire ( Applause. ) Mr. J. 0. PARR pr )posed that a vote of thaeks be given to Lord Newton and Colonel Pilkiogten for their iedresses on that occasisn. He felt that be was stand- ale in the piece of his son, whom they had honoured by appointing him as their Presidsnt, and who, if he only knew what was taking place that day, would very much regret h. was not amongst those present. But he wis somewhere between Japan and San Franefseo, and he was grail that even a telegram ver ul I not reach him. Thee were very pleased to welcome an old friend under a new name—Lord Newton—on his coming amongst them. He was present that afaerneon to show that he appreciated what had been done for him in the past, to show his 6.s7mpathr with the Conservative Party in War- rMgton and his ir t-ler: in the new Liberal Club. They were very pleased that his succssmor was Colonel Pi k-1 ingtnn, whose name was included in the resolution, wh was not a stranger to Warrington, tied who was always ready to come to Warriogton Oriel!) on any good ' , work which happened to be in progress. div.p: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Counc,l was held at the Waggon and Horses lan, on Tuesday evening. The President, Mr. A. C. Hinks, presided over a good attendance of delegates.
THE PROP iSED NEW MEETING ROM.

The follosving letter lunn toe Town Clerk (Mr. J. L. Whittle) was laid before the Council :—" Referring to your letter of the 13h of June Ids-, I am instructed by toe Town Hall,Pdrk and Baths Committee to inform you that they regret that they are unable to place a room at the Town Hall at your disposal for the meetings of your Association. The committee have frevently had to decline similar applications." The CHAIRMAN said that a minute was passed at the last meeting of the, Council to the effect that in the event of the app;ication b ing refused the Secretary should ask for perini,sion for a deputation to wait upon the Committee. It was for the Council to say now whether they thought the deputation was neces- sary after receiving the letter from the Town Clerk, which h thought put the veto on getting a room in the Hall. He was of the Opinion that it wouid be useless to approach the Cimmittee on the subjnt. Mr. PODMORE thought it would be adviaable to send a deputation in order that the Council might know the reasons why the Committee could not place a room at their disposal. Mr. BATTEESBIt agreed with Mr. Podin^re's views. In several other t )was the Trades Councils were allowed to meet in the Town Hall.
It was decided that the Secretary should write to the Town Clerk asking that a deputation mi,2ht bP received.
THE STRIKE OF WIGAN COTTON OPERATIVES.

The CHAIRMAN read the following letter frem the Wigan and Dr=trict Trade 3 ard Lsbour Council : " Fellow Worke:s,—On behalf of the Textile Workers of Wigan, the above Csuncil appeal to the van i sus Trades Ueions for financial support in their endeavour to obtain their just and reasonable demands for an advance of wages, viz 5 per cent, fer the etrdroorn and spinning departments, and 10 per cent for the male cardroom workers, which has already been conceoed throughout Lancashire, with tire exception of Wigan District. When we consider that the cotton operatives of this district are pa.d from 25 to 40 pr cent belew other towns, we think you will agree with us that the present demand is a juse one. The strike has now entered on its eighth week, and owing to the heavy &sin on the funds of the different societies affected, we appeal to you on their beaalr to reader what assistance you possibly can to bring the strtugle to a successful issue. The Council have decided to Issue this appeal in order to avoid the iStue of separate appoatsr by the respective societies affected, viz., the Cardroom Society, the Spinners' SocietY, and the Weavers' Soeiety, and therefore all previsus appeals are annulled. Delegate are requested to bring thi 1 matter before the notice if their society,in order that a prompt response may be in ‘de. Remember he who gives quickly gives twice. Feeling assured you will readily recoeniss the necessity of giving this your earliest consideration in order to effectively uphold the cause for which the Unions are contendurff, and hoping to receive a favourable reply at your earli eit convenience. We remain, Yours in Unity, S. WALSH, president, P. PRESCOTT, secretary." It was decided to refer the communication to the societies affiliated with the Council.

STEERING between Scylla The General Election, and Charybdis is an operation the prophets are engaged in, for the benefit of Lord SALIsBuILY and the present Government. It is a difficult operation. If an election were held in October it would avoid the tumult of the London municipal and School Board elections in November. But there are elections going on for some time before November Ist, when the polling takes place in most provincial boroughs,and if the Parliamentary elections came off in the early part of the month the whole of October would be given up to politico instead of pleasure and country sports,as it usuallY is. Some of the prophets in London actually know so little of municipal elections that they think theY will occupy half the month of November instead of being over on its first day. But why clash with these elections at all, when the register will be old and there is ample time ahead? The Loiadoa prophet has his answer ready. There are the London County Council Elections in March, and a dissolu- tion must net clash with them for anything. It must be amusing to our readers that all these specula" tions and arrangements should turn upon the con- venience of London. Everything is to be done to oblige the London constituencies. It has never occurred to these wiseacres that the best we,' t° allow London to attend to its local affairs is to postpone the General Election and not to slip it ill between one kind of local election and another. There is no reason why the General Election should come off this year or next spring, and the pleading is always as if the Londoners were entitled to fix it so as to fit in with their local affairs. We deny that any such right exists, or that it is expedient London should suit its ovro convenience regardless of the rest of the countri• We just as strongly deny that any urgent 00°6'7: sity exists for an immediate dissolution, or that It would be in accord with high reasons of State policy. Certain electioneering experts, or would-b 9 experts, have settled that it would be inadvisable to wait until the war enthusiasm is dead, in ordeir that awkward questions and facts may be avoideui That is the policy, and a country rke can see through it. There is no pro found constitutional wisdom in it. Tbere is even a touch of the comic about it, and it reads as if the carnivals were to be connected with the elections, and the armoured trains and Preside KRUGER were to be parts of it and do duty for argument. But is the war and its constitutional settlement to last for the whole of the next Polio' went? Are thGre to be no big or little social rer I forms? Of course, the most pertinent question 0i all is, what does Lord SALISBURY think about the General Election? He might be shut up in Pekl° for all the part his views and opinions play in the matter. The London members have hardly taken thePREauER into aecount in their eagerness arrange everything to please them so beautifully. Yet the decision rests with him absolutely- 09 can forward the date or postpone it, or put all the prophets out. Hence one of them said naivelY yesterday: "The decision rests entirely with the Prime Minister, who will be guided in the course he may adopt by the general development clf affairs." How can the writer know what will guide Lord SALISBURY? He would like him to be guidea by the Landon members. But they wanted all election in June or July, and have not got it. They are probably as certain to be disappointed in the° other dates and predictions.

THE romance is dying awe- The Cost or War. Theflirore which marked the early stages of the Smith African campaign hes long since ceased to eicitit' We should all he glad if the war in South Africla were at an end. It has been a series of events calculated to make the most indifferent sensitive to human suffering. Our losses in some battles were very severe, and for the time being tile, losses were unavailing. Amongst the wouadee there were some remarkable recoveries. But whey we come to sickness we have a most lamentable story, the full bearing of which we do not Ye‘ comprehend. We have lost more men by enteric fever and other diseases than by the anomie bullets or shells. We did not expect thie unhappy result, but when war once begl°s there is always the unexpected. Nor need viB discuss the losses in the form of prisoners, though here, again, some of the glamour of war has bee° destroyed, and Yeomanry, Highland regiment* cavalry and Militia have shared the same fate. The cost of war presents itself in a variety of weYe't and the loss in men, though often the We painful, is seldom the only striking loss. The I°es in trade and commerce is very considerable' though it may be hidden for a time. The orditr ary object of the world is not to make war, but r live at peace with each other, and to engage trading operations, intended to meet each other wants. The war with China has made its influ; once felt in Lancashire at once. It will not affe, the British taxpayer quite so quickly. The milli; and a quarter required for (expenses will hav° be provided for temporarily, and probably by leeth The ten millions and a quarter mainly for Seuvi, Africa will be in addition to what/has been Pre ously raised by loan. The sum may represent e.al penditure up to the end of the current finaael Out year, as far as can be calculated at oresent. does as the Boer war drags considerably, and it edde° not seem likely to end just yet, or by any s the dramatic atroke,as we had all hoped might be
pal Lit )re
_dilL

case, we shall probably have to find further money later on. The actual total cannot be estimated just yet, but it will exceed that of the Crimean war. There is a hope that in China, aS in South Africa, the gross amount of war xpenditure may ultimately come back to us from the working of an indemnity. Unfortunately, Collateral expenditure for military objects always rises, and the remanets are often larger than we had foreseen. In this way war is apt to exceed in Cost all our most liberal calculations. Its destruc- tiveness to public and private property is consider- able. The sum total is lost at some point or other, and never recovered for the general purposes of trade and business. The world is always the Poorer in the end, and capital seldom recovers 'until years of industry have added their savings and profits. There are, doubtless, corresponding advantages on the other side, but we are not pro- posing to discuss them now. All we desire to pre- sent is the terrible cost of war, and the wisdom of avoiding it wherever we can, and of terminating it as quickly as possible.

ANY visitor to London who passes through the Strand about noon will distinguish it for two characteristics—the one transient, and belonging only to the spring, the other a constant procession all the year round. The first named class, it need hardly be said, is composed of those whom Charles Lamb tenderly called "the shining ones," the People who, enjoying a tranquil life and finding; their pleasure in religion, enjoy their own parti- cular dissipation at Exeter Hall. The other class is Made up of the young moths of both sexes who ,via the theatrical agents, are seeking the glow of the footlights. They are generally most unsuitable for the profession, and cause the agents a terrible amount of trouble before they can be dismissed, Girls with dolly faces, flaxen hair, or hair that ca be brought to that hue, a certain mediocre ability in singing and dancing, an indifferent education, and a dl3like of the discipline of c?mmoner callings; young men who have distinguished themselves in school recitations,slim in figure and noticeable in feature,though generally little weak in will power about the chin—these are the most frequent types to be spotted edging their way in and out of the more business-like crowd. It is so very difficult to make them under- 'nand the amount of probation they must undergo beforo they can hope to win the applause even of the gallery, much less of the stalls, and how few Can possibly be stars. Teem is a book lately Written for American aspirants, by Mr. Hubert, Which would be excellent reading for them. Mr. liubert gives the first place to strong physique,and another important pta.2e—think of it, ye senti- Mentalists!—to a good digestion. Then,in addition to personal graces, there is need, he holds, for a really excellent education and perseverance,as well aS power of concentration. Even then the profes• men has few prizes.

The cychway in its pure and original form, is tiot at all likely to flourish in this country. It Would not, it may be said with safety, snit the taste of E iglish riders in the least degree. Cyclists are sometimes accused of rushing through ex- quisite scenery, bead bent, attention absorbed by the act of pedalling and the necessity for keeping a look out, endeavouring to drive their machines at a rate as near record-breaking as the conscinns Presence of the rural policemen permits. Yet the English rider loves the fair green lanes of England, With their wild roses and their honeysuckle, and Willingly climbs the dusty roads of the downs for the sake, surely, of that won- derful vision of exquisite green slope and Waving cornfield. How, then, could he appre- ciate those elevated city tracks on which the Wheelnaen of the States are said to be setting eir hearts, narrow timber causeways heavily mnl`zsd on either hand, which you are entitled to 1188 on payment of a certain toll, "and ride up and down all day if desired," as the prospectus of .one of these inventions in California cradely puts ? The ordinary pedestrian, who grumbles at tunes about the clanger of cycling in the streets, though on the whole astonishingly few accidents occur, may give a sort of approval in theory to these evices ; the racing man might find them of use, but they would, we thing, receive little Patronage from other claims of cyclists. The A.merican cycleway may suit the genius of the -A.merican people; we do not want to see it in our land, disfighring our cities and countrysides with mules upon miles of" elevated road."

The annual meeting of the Northern Union has been held, but the expected important changes in the rules of the game have been rejected. There was a large majority in their favour, but as it was 40t quite a three-fourths majority the old rules are adhered to. The punt-out rule was the" bone Of contention," several variations of it being suggested. The committee proposed to revert to 415 yards' scrimmage—rather a retrograde step— but the bf-st suggestion was that of the Bradford Club, which combined both scrimmage and punt- out. When kicked in touch the ball was to be Punted out by the opposite side, but when carried in by a player al5 yards' scrimmage was recom- %ended, This rule would, we think, have worked very well, for it would have still peoalised kicking to touch and at the same time would not have robbed a man pushed in touch after a long run, of the value of his effort. Thirty-two to thirteen was the voting in favour of the proposed alteration, and it is unfortunate that the majority was not large enough. The same remark applies to the suggestion with regard to knocking-on, Which well deserved adoption, for it ignored that Inevitable knocking forward of the ball by the catcher, as long as it did not touch ground. At the same time it enabled the opposing side to pro- tit by the knock-on of an opponent. Much tine Passing and fielding of the oval is spoiled by the Present arbitrary knock-on rule, and the game Would have been improved to a great extent by the adoption of the amendment. The changes Will come in time, no doubt, hut we should very znuch hdve liked to see them in operation during the season so soon to commence.
