div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

The Volunteers Bill, which reached the coal- Inittee t.e.age in the early part of the we,:k and is Practically a Gevernment Bill, considerably alters What may be calleel "the charter" of the Citizen Army, It has been objected to on several grounds, even by veteran volunteers, who might be expected to welvme the introduction of more elasticity into the peieeiple by which the force is governed. Those Who have raised objections to the measure found numeroue representatives in the House of Commons 'lron the provinces, who were decidedly active in _llO guerilla work of criticism. The House as a body 90wever, has been disinclined to jeopardise a hill that may yet be whipped into a very serviceable enactment. It is not expected that the measure Will escape amendment in the House of Commons, and it has already received the sanction of the Rouse of Lords; but Mr Wyndham has been con- ciliatory enough not to press the sub-section which Provides that Volunteere nifty undenake to serve in 4./13- part ot the world; at any rate until the opinion of Volunteers returning from active service in South 4frica had been ascertained. Its proposals are con- aidered by some as of an omnibus variety,and it can lite,nrcely be said to have received all the support "at was expected. 121evonshire has now contributed the winner of ~ Quven's prize at the National Rifle Association .7et;-,ine on rive occasions. Colonel Pearse, and Pri- .4to Beek, of the Ist Devons, were both winners in Other years. Mr. Kerslake, a yet earlier Queen's triZßran, was also a Devonien, bat resided at ridgwater, and the 'Somerset Volunteers had the .jedit of his success. As usual in connecrien with tri matter, there has been no little curiosity as to 4'o Personal habits of the prize.winner whose orelye and skill bring him successfully through an ueal such as the contest involves. It sometimes PPens that the Queen's prize falls to a teetotaler (i),; non-smoker. Ward, who has gained it twice, I},ileither the one nor the other, oough, as one of me Sunday papers unnecessarily puts it, "Ile has

always had the good sense to take in moderation the good things of life." The same paper describes him as unmarried, which is a mistake. His wife shared with him the congratulations of his native county in 1897, as she is doing again now. Next to the Chinese Puzzle and the Boer game of hide and seek, the question which seems mostly to exercise the mind ot man is that of how to keep cool. At the London Hippodrome the management k•ep going by supplying fans and lemon squash ad lib,and at other houses of public entertainment, the managers have adopted the simpler metho I of clos- ing the doors. When this is d sue it is usual for the London artistes to fleck to the provinces,where there is reason to fear they are faring but little better. There are many suggestions as to the best and the most approved methods of keeping cool,and a medical authority sets forth the following, welch has at least the merit of being simple and inexpen- sive. Allow cold water from a tai to run on both wrists for a few minutes. This will have the effect of drawing the blood from the heal and gently cooling the whole system, "and will be found more beneficial than large quan- ' titles of cooling drinks." The later sug- gestion is "seasonable" and appears to be needed. The habit of consuming large quantities of iced liquids is peculiarly vicious, or indeed quantities of -quash of any kind. The man or woman who can drink least in hot weather is the most sensible as well as comfortable. Strong foods may with great advantage be avoided, and if we only knew how to make salads as our neighbours beyond the silver streak make them, we might even be happy. But it is still true that Englishmen, with rare exceptions do not know either hov to eat, drink or dress properly in hot weather. We go to extremes, con- sume too much cold meat, as if that would cool us, and invariably dress in clothing made of the wrong material. We have been told over and over again that wool is the proper thing to battle with the heat wave in, bat somehow, while accepting the doctrine as a rule we do not accept it so as to profit thereby. Swindon has reason to feel proud of its police force, from the point of view relating to the physique of its members; though there are other towns in the provinces that might possibly vie with even Swindon. The Wiltshire constabulary has long been noted as including many very tall men. At toe Swindon inspection the other day,by Captain &erne, R.N., it was shown that the av-rage height of thirty men on parade was sfc 11 7-10chs inches; twelve of them being six fee or more, and the tallest (P.C. Millard) 6ft 3 inches. The superin- tendent of these men stands 6 feet 2 inches without boots. One would like to hear of a finer set in the provinces. _

It appears that the average price of wheat for the whole of last year is 25s 8.1. This, with two exceptions, 1894 and 1895, is the lowest annual average recorded in a whole series of 120 years for which official prices are available. The annual average price of wheat recavered in 1898 to 343 par quarter, which formed the feature of most intens. in the corn market of that year But it was not maintained in 1899, and a year of mall fluctuations and a low general level followed one which showed remarkably wile variations, rising to a quotation of 4Ss in the month of May, but relapsing after harvest to 25i 51.

One of our most prominent physicians. Sir Dyce Duck worth,has been saying that he thinks we give toe little at-ention to the important question of proper burial. There is a finality about te)e process which he advocates, that of crenweion, welch, doubtless, has much to eommend 111, when con- sidered in connection with the burial of persons who have died of small-pox or other infectious disease. But we are told by Sir Dyce that embalm ing is really cheap, and, if so, there are those who pass into the unseen of old age or accident who might with advantage, perhaps, be made subjects of that ancient an i venerated process. The sug- gestion, at any rate, serves to remind us of how much these ancient Egyptians were in advance of ourselves on this point. votwithstanding all that is said on the subject of the best means of dispos- ing of the dead, we do not get excited over it as in other matters, but have the satisfaction of knowing that funerals,at least,are not so costly as they were. Excellent as the boat arrangements are un ler the existing Post Office system, there are many towns in the wivisces, or clusters of towns or of villages, that Night be vastly benefited by a scheme such as that at Huddersfield, where in one week eleven thousand letters were placed in the letter boxes of the Corporation tramcars for cenveyance from the suburbs to the General Post Offics there. The same scheme, of course, would not suit any and every locality. But the success which attends the system in operation at Huddersfield, and some other places, is full of suggestiveness as to what might be done elsewhere, either by the governing bodieP, or by others having the general interests of the com- munity at heart. -

Ilan-Chester and Brighton, if no other city or town in the provinces, are to nave the honour very shortly of a visit by the Shah in Shah, Ring of Kings. He is one of the most enlightened of Eastern Potentates, perhaps the most learned of them all, as well as the wealthiest. Yet Persia is one of the decaying nations of tbe world to which Lord Salisbury referred some time since, and Europe has her eye upon it. It does not need very keen eyesight bo perceive that within a few years the country governed by the learned Shari will be a theatre in which diplomatic victories will be lost and won. Rightly or wrongly, Russia is credited with something more than a mere desire to gain a paramount position in Persia. Hitherto, like Ntoroccri, she has escaped because each of the great Powers as over the China business, distrusts the other, and is waiting to see who will be bold enough to start the scramble.

When the question was raised in Bristol County Court the other day, as to what constitutes "a menial," the learned Judge took the great Black- stone's ruling that a menial servant is one who resides within his master's walls. Counsel conten- ded that lexicographers were not agreed upon that interpretation, and that Blackstone had no philo- logical basis for his view of the meaning of the word. According to Judge Au•tin's view the menial is entitled to a month's notice; the word implies no slur, and the man stands on a better footing than one with weekly wages.

At ttunc-irn on Friday, Pater Rice, a hawker, of [Teach-road, was summoned fir assaulting his father, Charles Rice, also a hawker. 4r J liurton defended. The father alleged that on Monday, be- , cause he comolained that tile prisoner had nut brought sufficient grass for a foal, the prisoner aimed a blow at his head with a large piece of wood. Phe father guarded his head with his arm, which was broken below the elbow. The defence was that the father was the aggressor, and had aimed a blow at his son's neck with a " i," au agricul- tural implement, which would have gone througl-s nim had he not caught it with his hand. son described his father as a roaring madman, who had made his living by fighting, and ne struck him in self-defence only.—The father said he would be con- tent IF his son was beund over, and he was bound over accordingly for six months.

Bowlers in Runcorn ditrrict were provided with an interesting match on Saturday at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point. Levi Fowler, greenrnan the hotel coneeded Thomas Dean of Runcorn 10 points in a game of 81 for £lO aside, and the encounter was witnessed by a crow I woich taxed the accommodation of tbe green to the utnan4t. A splendid game was witnessed. Ar. half time Levi had wipNl off five of his arrears and shor,ly after resuming the game was recorded 47 all. Levi now forged ahead but Dtqw had a remarkable run of 14 and again drew clear, but Levi was not to be shaken off and the players peeled at 76, 78, 79 an 80. At the last end Levi stood two in, close umand Dean playing through with a beautiful throw, took the jack and won a moat exciting match by one point, Mr Robert Wright efficiently performed the duties of referee and stake holder. A point of great interest to brewers and licensed victuallers was raised at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. before Messrs. Ja13288 Handley and William Handley when application was made for permission to sell under a license previously held by James Spann at the Albion Inn, Nelson-street. Mr W Handley pointed out that this house had been closed for some months and Spann had since kept another house called the Three Crowns in King-street where he bad died. A man was not allowed to hold two licenses and this license could not be transferred from Spann. Mr. Handley inquired whether any hard- ship had been felt since teis house was shut up.— Superintendent Pearson : No sir; not that. lam aware of.—Mr W Handley: Would it not be hettQr to leave the house as it is until the annual lie, w- ing sess'ons which take place in a few weeks. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Warrington.

RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A CORRHSPONDENT]. The Population Question.

To be" hauled over the coals "is not a process that is enjoyable at any time; though, when there is ju.Atice in the cause for " the hauling,' the sufferer can philosophically put up with it. A writer in last week's issue of the "Runcorn Examiner" fancies he has cs.ught me napping, and draws attention to 'significant figures" which I apparently overlooked. Runcorn (Urban District) population at censu, 1891-20.050; estimated popu- lation in middle of 1899-19,000." The writer then draws his own "obvious conctusion" " that Runcorn as a town and community is in a parlous state. Nine years of uninterrupted prosperity in the country generally; the advent of the Snip Canal with its attendant commerce ; and yet, the popu- lation of a town so favourably situated as Runcorn is, has, instead of increasing, decreased by 1,050' 'Tis all, no doubt, a beautifully obvious conclusion, and would have been well had it sopped there; but no! oa it goes: "The Medical Ufficer of Health attributes it to the ' deuressed state of trade locally," and he is unquestionably right in his judgment. As the remainder of the note is a de- duction upon the above basis, by dealing with the basis I shill cover all the ground, so for the present will quote no further.

Let us take the hiitory of the town and com- munity of Runcorn in de,iadoe and we find: In 1801 the Pepueitioa was 1,474; in 1811, 2060. ;in 1821. 3,103 ;in 1830, 4 500 ; in 1841, 6 000 ;in 1851 8.688 ; in 1861, 10,063 ; in 1871, 12,414; andoin 1881, 15,133; decidedly continuous and steady growth. An average for the whole of the periods named would give U 8 slightly over 1,500 of an increase for ea&a decade. Pie)gression at the same rates would therefore, give us at the close of two more decade .4 (1991) 18,133. But what do we actually find ? " Estimated population in the middle of 1899 19,030." An even greater increase! This sufficiently demonst.rares that progress has been maintained by Runcorn, both as a town and as a community. As I 'quote my antagoni-t for the ;Last figure, the estimate of 1900 is common ground between us. Surely, tnen it is obviotee: that the cause whichihrings the population from 15,133 in 1881, to 20,050 in 1891 (the last census),is to be looked for somewhere out- side the realms of ordiciary progression. As a, matter of fact, it was due to the Ship Canal under- taking; at which time—(according to the evidence of one of the census enumerators of 1891, whom 1 interviewed)—Runcorn hal a floating population of about 3 500; and, these toe,were mostly men whose employment in the excavation of the Ship Canal nece-si:ated their residing in Runcorn The same gentleman also tells me that £5,000 a week was paid in wages to these people. We can further cerreborate this. Granting that in the decade 1881 te 1891, the town and community made the same progress, and 1,500 were added to the population at the end of that ;«icsde ; we would have, with the addition of 3,503 (ft )ating population),slightly more rhea 20,050 the figure quoted as the official census return for 1891. Naturally, when the Ship Canal was completed those dependent upon it vanished, and within a twelve-month afterwards the pepu- ',diet' came nearer to its normal condition ; still it never fell below it. This should sufficiently illus- trate that at least I thoueht the figures anything hut " eignifieant " as evidence ot the contention put forward by the writer quoted.

Now to deal with the a-sertion that I have been "ever urging the loc tl anthorVy to spend with a free- domlhardly justified by the commercial I.r mperity of the town." I don't, want to quibble about terms,and it is true I have been urging the Council to spend money; and will continua to urge them to do so. Bit that. I have ever advocated the squandertng of money I deny. I have told the Ruacorn Urban District Council that in the past they have made oad bargains; and have urged them to relinquish that policy. I have told them in principle: "We paid a3s 31 rate for 'next to nothing,' and have argued we would willingly bear a 33 5d rate for 'something.'" Furtiermore, whenever the Council nave acted in accord with what I have urged—and they have done so more than once or twice—neither the Council nor the ratepayers have had occ.;asion to rt gret.

A. word, in conclusion, ahout liedical Officers' re- ports or rather the wordy hypothesis of opinions which comii iindtsr that title. The reading of a series of them shows that the general run of Medical Officers know as much about trade as a polar bear knows about brick-bats. And, if Dr. McDougall attri hates the decrease of 1,050 in the population in the last eight years to the "depressed state of trade locally" in his report to the County Medical Officer Elealth, it simply proves an utter ignorance on his pan', of the cumrnon history of Runcorn in the fist instance; and it is irreconcilable with his re- port issued to the Urban District Council of Run- corn at their meeting on April sth last.

Our correspondent has gone to a lot cf trouble to prove Runc3rn's prosperity in the face of such tow?. odds as a decrease in population for the last eight years, but he has not in the least altered our nninion t ,at the figur•.s quoted last week, viz.. 1891- 20_050; 1899-19 000,a,re significant. Their significane3 °opt to beapnareit to tho most obtuse intelligence Granted that Runcorn's population to-day shows an increase of 1 500 per decade for the last hundred years, what areument on behalf of the town's pr,splritv is this in the face of the indisputable fan'. that eight years ago the population was 1,050 more than now? In business, a man whose returns showed a corresponding de- crease after eight years' hard work would be considerably dis,urbPd by the prospect before him. Dr MlDougall seems to have come in for an unwarranted attack merely because be ventured to a. tribute the decrease to local trade depression, aolut which we con.i ler a man in his position has every qualification for exnressine an opinion. A eltnce at the columns of the " Examiner "for the past few years will corroborate his statement for there is viper of evidence there that Runcornians have frequently been mere than a little alarmed by the trade which has gone away from them.fluncorn's lack ot progress has ben almost a bye word in the p‘st,and the decrease in population is an indication that things commercial are even yet far from being what they should be—En." Examiner,"]

The Warrington to Runcorn Light Railway scheme has, so the promoters intimate, been aban- doned for a time. This is a course, no doubt, due to the collapse of the Warrington to Northwich Light Railway scheme. ,One scheme possibly affected the other to a greater extent than. the unitiated would imagine. No one seems a degree sorry at its abandonment. The one feature Runcorn people looked forward to was the possibility of opening out Weston P lint, but when that idea was abandoned their interest in the concern ended

rootpath obstructions are a source of real annoy- ance to pedestrians, but occasionally they have be- come absolutely dangerous. Writing for the present from memory I cannot be sure that the Runcorn Urban District Cauncil have adopted any Town's Police Clauses Act which woul make it an offence against the peace of her Majesty's subjects to render footpaths almost impassible by the display of goods, or the piling op of empties outside buginess premises. The chief offenders in this respect are the tradesmen in the vicinity of the lower part of Bridge-street and should this paragraph meet their eye, they might consider the feelings of passengers a little more and abate the annoyance. The cause of my writing in this strain is due to the numerous complaints I have received.

The Frodsham Bench have shown that they at least can get behind a "man's conscience." Some time ago, an application for an exemption from vaccination was applied for by a man named Davies on behalf of his little child. He attended the court and applied in the usual way for the certificate. De had a conscientious objection, and thought vaccination would be injurious to his child and though he asserted his conscientiousness upon oath the bench declined to admit that the man had a "conscientious objection and refused the applica- tion. The sequel was enacted at the last sessions at Frodsham, on Wednesday, when Davies was fined Li—judgment, going by default—for neglecting to have hi child vaccinated within the prescribed time. Truly the Vaccination Act is a farce, or its applica- tion can be made so by prejudice, Its intention wss, no doubt, to provide a looplele tor those per- sons who objected to the operation; but here we see that a person who sweara to having a "conscien- tions objection "—no matter what that may mean, the applicant swore be had got it—is simply disbelieved and has to suffer in consequence.

A VIOLENT SEAMAN ASSAULTS THE RUNCORN Potac

Two seamen of the " Dors6t," now lying at Run- corn Dock,, were brought up in custody. before &iessre A. R. Norman -(pre.iding), and Mr Elandley. on :..laturday last. Henry Conway, was charged wi h being drunk and disorderly, and with assiult hag P.C. Gilpin whilst in the execution of his duty, the previ eysn,ng. John Williams, his comrade, was charged with drank ani disorderly conduct on the same occasion.—lt appeared that P.C. Gilpin saw the prisoners come out of the " Holybeal fiarboar," and Conway he noticed behaved in a dis- gusting mannsr on the footpath. Witness cautioned him about it, but the only notice prisoner took was to use filthy language, go higher up the street and repeat the offence. Prisoners then proceeded to the Stanley irms and asked for two pints of beer but the barmaid refused to supply them Prisoners again misb shaving themselves witness took Conway in custody. Prisoner resisted all he could and assaulted him about the lers with his feet, and struck him on the shoulder with a pint bottle filled with b ter. P.O Bowyer coming up took charge of Williams. Conway was so violent that assistance had to he obts,ined.before he was lodged in the cells. —George Smith, a young man who a.sisted the corroborate4.—P C. Bowyer proved the. c 559 against Williams.—Both prisoners were tined 5s and 7s costs for being drunk and disorderlv. Annual Prize Distribution. Address by Mr. Roger Bate, C C. Tbe annual distribution ot priz s to the successful scholars of the Runcorn Institute Diy Scheol took place in the new wing of the Institute, which had been taste- fully decorated, on Wednesday afternoon. The chair was taken by Mr W, Handley (Chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Council) and he was supported on the platform by Mr Roger Bate, JP., C.O (deputy chairman of the Cheshire County Council Technical instruction , Committee) who came especially for the purpme of dis- tributing t e prizes, Mr Simnel Taylor, J.P., E unison. C.C., ani Mr TA. Lawrenson, M.A. (headmaster). There was also a fair number of parents present. Ih3 oth r members of the teaching staff who were present included: —Messrs H C Mayston,B.A. W ScrunFeour, J T Irving; Miss A Johnson (mistress of tit° preparatory school) and Miss Globe (teacher of cookery). Mr. W. Handley on taking the chair said he could not but express his pleasure that for the first time in the history of the school one of the members of the Cheshire County Council had favoured them with his presence. Be was of course excluding their own local County Councillors. Mr. Bate now deliv.ered an address in which he drew ettention to the maener in which the funds devoted to Heichnical instruction became vested in the County C ouncil. I i some counties this money was used for the relief of rates, but from the first Cheshire County Council had spent the whole of the money for the advancement of technical instructico. In the days of the late Mr. Philip Speakman, who was a member of the County Council Committee and who was invariably deeply interested in all that concerned Runcorn, the committee when the fund the:: Runcorn was prepared not only to ceotribut ! from the rates, but also to make tree contribution for technical instruction work, they were most anxious to do all they could to encourale the work in Rencorn. The committee had watched with vere derp interest the progress made in Runcorn. They were all very much indebted to Sir John Brunner for the del) interist he had taken in the work of er?ucetion. in the County of Cheshire, and Rene orn had felt the infteence of that great life not only in its business but upon its educational movements. When they re- membered Runcorn's long history and the great changes through which the town had passed and knew the pcoition the town held te-day,they all ought to be proud, and he was pleased for the first tim3 to distribute the przs in Runcorn's secondary school. He hoped the headmaster's rep-rt would inithe future show an increase in numbers and an equal excellency of results. They could not over esti nate the value of brain power to a nation. If England's commercial progress had to he coetinued, if its commerce had to be extended, if the people were to be fully employed, if the present rste of wealth had tea be maintained in the future as in the past it would be by the he% s and girls who were in our schools to day, who had talent and b-ain power that this would be accemplished. (Applause ) Re hoped the secondary schools of the nation would shortly be in the position of having scholarships that would carry the clever hoes from the schools to the Uoiversitii s• The County Council had established a great number of scholarships and he was glad to find there were in the Runcorn school ten scholars who had won elementary schotsrships. Dealing with his visit to Runcorn Mr. Bate paid that what he had seen in the town would make him go back with the impression that all the money the County Council Tsclinical Instruction Committee had RI freely grant ei to Runcorn had been wively and well spent. Upon resuming his seat Mr. Bate was loudly applauded. Mr. E. In3ison, C.C., in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Rare, paid a very high tribute to his work as an educationeliet, and also to the generous and courteous manner he always inclined to petitions from Runcorn for aid. He elan concurred with the reference Mr. Bate had made to the provision of the missing link between the secondary and university schools. (Applause) Mr. S. Taylor seconded the vote of thanks, and re- minded him that if Runcorn people were not acquainted with himself personally, they were frilly conversant with his work. (Applause.) The vote weir heartily accorded and briefly reepandecl to.
A vote of tharka was also accorded to the Chairman, and the assemble adjourned to view an exhibition of coctery and woodwork.
WARRINGTON Music in the Park.

On Sunday afternoon the Buckley-street Sunday School Band will render the following programme: —March, " Woodinancote." J Jubh ; selection, " William Tell," Rossini ; anthem, " I will lift up mine eyes," Dr Clarke; selection, " Verdi," H Round ; air variation, " Rousseau's Dream," If Round, Mr .T T Richqrdson will conduct,

St, Paul's Choir at Blackpool. The choir of St. Paul', Church, to toe number of 38, had a trip to Blackpool on Monday. Accom- panied by the Vicar (the Rev. E. R.Tarbuck)and the organis:-, (Mr. Wilkes), the party left Bank Quay Station at 7.34. their destination being reached after a pleasant journey at 8.50. All dispersed to spend the morning according to their respective inclina- tions, but met by arrangement at 12,30 at the Pavilion Buildings, where Mrs. Taylor had provided an excellent lunch,which was much enjoyed. Visits to the Tower, Wh.-el, bathing and sailing occupied the afternoon until tea time had been reached when all again assembled at the Pavilion. The train was boarded at 8.29 and Warrington was safely reached, shortly before ten o'clock, the time in the saloon passing too quickly owing to the excellent pro- gramme of music which was gone through.

div.head: RUNCORN BOATMEN HEAVILY
div.p: RUNCORN BOATMEN HEAVILY
FINED.
Pilfering Coal from Narrow Boats.

At the Runcnrn Police Court, on Saturday, b,fore Messrs. A R Norman (presiding) and VVilliam Handley, a father and on (Charles and Eiward Osborne) were charged with stealing two tons (..t coal, valued 181 s. thei property of 51,-,84:8 Simpson. Davies and Son, at Runcorn. between the 28:b January 1899 and the 28. h of June 1900.

James Higgins, outdoor foreman for Messrs, Sinapson, Davies and Soo, testified to the fact that his employers got their coal from the Astley, Tyldesley, Coal and Salt Company, sun also from the Bridgewater Trustees, Woreler The coal was conveyed by narrow boats from the collieries to Runcorn. The elder prisoner was captain of the boats " Milo " and " Midas ' and the younger prisoner was his hand. They were engaged by his firm to carry coal from tbe collieries to Ruucarn. For several sears they had been obliged to complain to tbe colliery proprietors of shortages; especially during the last 12 or 18 months. During some months their shortages had been nine or ten tons. The colliery proprietors al ways assured them that they had their !full quantity, and blamed their employ es for the stort- ' ages. On Saturday, the 30cn June, witness visited the residence of the prisoners at Stone-bills, Haltou-road, in company with Sergeant Gregory. Thsy also visited two stables, and some empty houses. Witness saw there about three tons of coal in lumis and about 10 cwt. of slack. The matorial was similar to that which his employers dealt in. Boat people were allowed to burn coal on their boats, but were forbidden to carry any laway. Having stiff -red from the loss of coal the matter was put in the hands of the p)lice. James Sumner' mate of the narrow boats" Mite" and 1" Midas " swore he had been in the employ of Charles lOsborne, on and off, during the last 13 years. Be had served the last 18 months continueus'y with him. When they were lying at the Dock, witness generally went to 0 aborne's for his meals. At the elder prisoner's requen he had taken barrows full of coals and slack to his house, and, also, to the stables where it was stored. All of it was taken from the boats, and he (wituess) knew it belonged to Simpson Davies and Son. Since the pri- soners were locked up witness stated he had "a dog'- life "of it with Mrs o‘borne. She had threatened to "do for him," and blamed him for telling the police that pee goners had false keys for the empty houses. tie bact also been asked to clear out iA* country, hut be was determined to tell the truth in Ito matter. William Henry White, aged 13 years, residing with hia mother at 56, Halton-road, stated that he had known the prisoners Charles Osborne and his son Edward when they lived at the Big House, at the bottom of Robert- street. He then saw them on several occasions taking coal from tneir boats and carrying it up filbert-street to the backyard of their house. Since they had been living at Wickstone Hill witness had seen both Cnarles and his eon Edward many times whee'ing coal in a barrow from their boats towards their houses. On several occasions he saw the big white mule attached to a barrow pulling it up the hill. The barfows sometimes contained lumps and sometimes slack. He had also seen th(m taking big stone flags and small setts in a barrow covered ov. r with slack. On Thursday, the 2Etb June last, witness was sitting on the canal wall with Charles France when he saw the prisoners on their boats. He saw a woman come down to the boats, and bear& her say to the Osborm's " Pat it in the first stables," and at the same time he saw her give the prisoners a key. The prisoners then gct some short pieces of wood and put them on a barrow. They placsd a bagful of wood on the top, and wheeled it up the hill towards their house. Retire they started Charles France asked prisoners;to give him a bit. The prisoner Edward replied "We have to buy thie." Shortly afterwards a tittle woman brought the barrow back. Mrs. o,borne was on the boat dating the whole time. Every time witeesa had seen Osborne' boats coming along the canal he had seen them wheeling something towards their house. Charles France, residing with his father at 9, Porter- street, Runcorn, s-ated *bout 12 months ago he was is Halton-road, aria saw Edward Osborne and another maw wheeling a barrowtul of coal from their boats towards Osborne's house. The elder prisoner was putties the coal into the barrow and the other was handing it to him out of the boat. He also corroborated the previ- ous witness.

William Fisher, of II ,lton-road,agent for the property on Wickstono Hill, teatifiid that 7, 9 and 13 were the houses occupied by the Osborne'e. They beireaged to William Elliott, No. 3, Springfield-place, Sutton Coal Fields, Warwickshire. The houses 1, 3 and 5 belongedr to Miss Eiliott,of the same address. Osborne had us authority to use any of the ematy houses for storage purposes, and had not been supplied with any of the doorkevs of those houses Osborne paid his first rent oo the Ist of February, 1899. P.C. Carrington, on the 29:h of June, in company with Sergeant Gregory visited some of the empty houses and stables at Wickstone Hills, Halton-road. In a cot- tage near to where the prisoners lived they found about 35 owt of coal. In the next house there would no about 10 or 12 cwt. In the stable on the opposite side there would be about 15 cwt, and in the top stable- toere was quite a ton of coal. On the 30th June, when the prisoners were committed on another charge, wit- ness asked them how they accounted for so much coal being in the stables and the empty houses. Each of them replied. "It's what we have taken from the boats be!onß- ing to Simpson Davies,when tied up at Halton-road,frots time to time." Wituess also asked if they could tell him of any person from whom they had purchased coal. The elder prisoner replied: "I do not know anyone. Ido not remember buying any coal for a long time." The younger prisoner made a similar reply. P.C. Wilding stated that on the previous day be re- ceived the prisoners into custody from the linutsford polioe. He brought them to Runcorn, and charged them with the present charge. Charles 03borne replied : "I can't say anything more; only the statement I have made before" The son said he had nothing to say. Both prisoners pleaded guilty, and were each fined 50s. or one month hard labour. The mo ler was paid.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
SAVAGE ASSAULT.-A MAN STRUCK ON THE HEAD WITH A BRIDLE.

At the Warrington Police Court yesterdar, Richard Wethngs, 63,Nicholson-street,was summoned for ass iult- mg Frederick Massey, 31, Heath-lane, on the 14th July. —There was a cross summons against Massey for assauPing Wettings. —Mr. Browne appeared on behalt ~1 Massey and Mr. Forshaw represented Wellings.—Mr. Browne said the case was not one of ordinary assault but of cieldrrately hitting a nun on the head with a bridle with fourrings and a bit weighing nalf a pound. Mr. Mussy was a tuechanic in the employ of the Whit, - cross Company and on Friday morning shortly teem 8 o'clock he was washing himself preparatory to going to work. He heard two dogs fighting and on going out found his dog and the defendant's dog fighting. De- fendant's dog was pinning Msssey's dog and his WU, boy against the wall. Complainant kicked both the dogs and got the boy away. Toe dogs then ran into an open space and began fighting again. Comrlainant followed them and tried to seps rate them. Wellirgs came our nd said" Will you kick my dog ?" and Massey replied "Take your dog away.' He then stooped down, and took bold of the dogs and whilst be stooped Welings hit him on the head with a bridle, The blow stunned him, and the blood rushed out, saturating his clothing. He had to be taken to the Infirmary and attended to by Dr. Battle. The doctor said it would be at least a week I or ten days before the wound was better. There was no assault by Massey in any shape or form.—Evidence was given by complainant, who in cross-examination admitted that be went to Llandudno the same day. He denied striking Wettings in the face.—For the defence, Mr. Forshaw :said that the complainant came to the def ndant'a yard•on Saturday morning and set his d, g fighting with the defendant's. He found that his dog was getting the worst of it and began kicking Wettings' dog, He kicked it several times and Wehings thereupon did hit him on the head with the bridle but it was not a severe blow. Complainant retaliated by striking Wet- tings in the face. Complainant provoked the whole thing and deserved what he got.—Evidence was given in support ;:of this statement.— the magistrates c ,n- -sidered the assault upon Massey a most unprovol- ed one and fined Wettings 40s and costs. The cross summons was dismissed with costs. SMART FINE FOR HOBBERT.—A SAD CASE

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, before *- F. Monks and other magistrates, Henry Lumbey, 18, Scott-street, was charged on remand with stealkg from the cash drawer in the chief clerk's office in the goods department at the Central Station, at 4 20 on Thuralay morning,64 the money of the Cheshire Lines Committee. —Mr, T. S. Steel represented the prisoner and pleade guilty.—Mr. Simpson, who prosecuted on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Committee said the prisoner came into the employ of the committee in March lest He was at firs employed,in the chief clerk's office but lately he was transferred to the shipping office in the ,tame buildieg All went well until the beginning of May when rnoees was -niseed from the cash drawer. On the fir .t flay of Mar 4s 4d was missing, on the 6th 19, on the 12th £1 3. 6d, on the 28th 23 7d, on June lst 93. July 17,h 6, an - on the date in question 65 si. On each occasion th money had been locked up safely in the drawer at night by the chief clerk and on the following morning he had found the drawer locked but the money was missing Evidently some eerson had had a key to &- the drawer. Inquiries were made and suapicions were attached to the prisoner. Money was nne left' in the drawer for two or three weeks and the prisoner went on his holidays. Money Was ph.c.d in the drawer during his absence and nothing WaS missed. The first night he returned money was put in the drawer and was missed on the fello wing m lesing. Money was then marked and left in the drawer. During the night an inspector concealed him self in the office and at 4.20 in the morning the prisoner c3me in, unlocked the drawer, took out the money and locked the drawer. The Inspector seized him whilst he had the money and key in his banal.—For the def. n Mr. Steel said it was an extremely sod can. Tne prieziner was only thirty years of age and was very well connected, his father holding a very good position in Burton as a goods agent for the Midland Railway Co. Prisoner was a married man with two young children. He was engaged directly by Mr. Meidrum on very good rec mmendations. He bad been employed by Messrs. Lever Brote, at their branch in Belfast and he came from Bear, to enter upon his employment in Warrinston. He had a very comfortable home, he did not drink or elmtlF, and be could not understand why he had corn. nutted the offence. He assured him (Mr. Steel) that he had never taken anethieg from the. till bet ore. On being asked by him (Mr. Seel) for an explanation he said "I can- not tell why I did it. A sudden temecat ion came over me and I could not resist it." His wife gave as her only explanation that he hed been away during the week and had left her with only 6i. The Cie shire Lines Corn- mitre kept- a week in hand. The vaife grumbled at him leaving her with such a small amount and when he went into the office the temptation came over him, he had a y in his pocket, which he tried in the drawer. Unfortunately it fitted and he took the money. He hoped the magistrates would take the circumstances into con- sideration and submitted that the cafe, could be dealt with under the First Offenders' Act.—ln answer to the Chairman, Mr. Simpson said the committee pressed the case as stigma had been thrown on other clerks. They had reasen to believe that the other amounts of money had been taken by the prisoner.—The Bench decided to fine the prisoner £5 with the alternative of a month's imprisonment.

ROBBING A SLAT GAS METER.—James Devereux, 10 years of age, was charged with stealing from a slit gas meter in the dwelling•house of Charles Higginson.Porter-street, Bove- time between 2 and 4.30 pm on Friday 988 d in lash,the money of Charles Hankineon.— Sverint-ndent Monaghan stated that at two o'clock the pro-ecuts,r, who was a gas stoker.went to bed. He got up at 4.30 and noticed a poker lying close to the meter. He also found the broken ionic of the meter on the floor. Nothing was heard until 6 o'clock when prosecu- tor's son saw the prisoner and ascertainet that he had been spending money very fre ly. Prisoner ran away when he saw the prosecutor's son, but he was caughe and is 6d was found in his possession. Prisoner admitte i stealing the amount mentioned in the charge from the meter.—The magistrates sent the lad to a refearm ttory far five years. ASSAULT ON A WORKS MAN 4 GER —Henry Owen was charged on a warrant with assaulting Wiliam Henry Atkin on the Nth inst.—Mr Browne, instructed by the T amen- lane Tanning Company, prosecuted. He sta ed that the prieurysr was employed at the tannery and in consequence f his not coming to work on Monday as he was drinking, Mr Atkin the manager, •• sacked" him as well as ttaree others. The men met the man who hat been engaged in prisoner's place on Tuesday. and asked him if he knew what a " soak " was (meaning that they would put him in a pit.) The man replied that he did and they told him they would put him in a pit if he did not stop work. They followed him Into the works and the man was so afraid that eaamplaine to 'Mr Atkin Mr Atkin came on ths scene and found the prisoner under the influence of d ink. He hat no right on the premises and Mr Atain asken hi rn three time to go away but he refused. Mr Atkin then got hold ot him to put him out and the prisoner g t him by thi shoulders and puled him down. Mr Atkin strong, ant the prisoner being under the influence of drink he got tWs .mastery over the man —Thomas Bibby, another employe was then charged w;th assault,ng lidward Baker.—Complainant in evidence admitted that h struck the prisoner first —Mr Browne withdrew he case on the prisoner giving an un se-taking not to repeat his conduct. -w-n was fi id 20e and costs (21 123 )d in all), with the option of a month's imprisonment. man) J. J. Cr ,sfield and Murray. A CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECToR FlNED.—Willivn Edward Davies, of if'rodahano. was surnm-med by Thom-s Riley. Riley stated that the defendant had applied to that Court upon a previous oacasio n for an exemption under the consoience Obtuse " ad it had been refused —Defendant was flied 21. NEGLIGENT DRIVERS —Rdward Hunt, of Heisby, was fined 5s for driving a horse and Inrry without a light on the 23rd June; and Patrick O'Don dd. of Warrington, wis fined 5s for being asleep Whilst in charge of a horse and lurry.— John Bright White, a firmer, of Dunham Hill, was fined be. for allowing ten cows to stray on the Highway, at that place, on the 14th July—Defendants pleaded gailty in all these eves. STEiLING FROM THE PERSON jr PRODSHLM.—WiIIISM Caldwell, and N''..ary Caldwell, tramps, both old offanders, pleaded guilty to stealing £7 10s. from the person of William Warburton of Kingsley, on the 17th of July. and also to rec-iving the same knowing it to be sto:en.—From the evi- den •e. it would appear that the prisoners had gone to the " Cheshire Cheese" Inn. Frodsham, on that date, and whilst they were there Warburton came in. They entered into con- versation and the female prisoner alleged Warburton wanted to spend the night with her, and gave her certain moneys to entice her to do so, The female and Warbarton had gone in the direction of Synagogue Well for some "bad purpose." and was there she hail robbed him of the money.--Rvidence of the parties being seen to,ether was iven by Harry Forster, and Forster. 1 ndlo,el and landlady of the " Cheshire Cheese ;" John amelow, 14 loam Terrace. baker ; and nily Brovn. wife of Thomas Brown, Cliff View.— P.C. Thomas Roberts. testified to the apprehension of prisoners, bat the money was not found upon them.—Both prisoners pleaded extenuating circums,ances, stating that but for Warburton'a temptation, they would have gone on their way. —The Cnairman agreed that it might have been so; and, added, that Warburton had made a "fool of himself."— Qmaitioned as to what they had done with the money, prisoners replied they had thrown it away before they were arrested. -Both were sent to prison for 4 calendar months with hard labour.

Good Tem plary. The usual weekly meetiug of the Temperance Mission lodge of the 1.0,0.1. was held in Brick- street schoolroom. Bro J Sheath presided, four visitors being present from the Warrington "On- ward lodge and one from Swinton. Three members were re-admitted into membership. Bro Cliv,ham (Swinton) gave a short address on the good of the Order. The fAlowiniz programme was then ren- dered. Bro Wright song, " The Fisherman and his Child," Sister tip,trkes sang, " Never from Thee :" Bro Clipstiam reading "The Mysterious Guest ;" Bro Wright recitation, "Courting Incidents ;" Bro J Sheath recitation, " Psalm of Life ;" Bro Clipsham song "Marching on;"and the visitors were thanked on behalf of the lodge by Bro J Sheath, after which the lodge was closed.

div.head: Lett to the Cbttor.
div.p: Lett to the Cbttor.
The Lack of Lighting in Orford-lane
Wa—rringto—n.

Sir,—l observed in your issue of the Th mat, thet one of the Town Councillors drew the attention of the Council to the urgent need for better street lighting in Orford-lane, and described the condition of things as " A scandal." I tnink the gentleman might well have gone one better, and described it as criminal neglect. How much longer this nond.tion of things is to be tolerated by the inhabitants of the two wards, divided by Orford-lane, I for one have little idea, but I venture to think that the sooner the electors arouse themselves from their apathetic condition.and begin to consider the source from which this indifference arises, and the possibilities before them,the sooner we are likely to have our wards put into the condition we would have them In the two wards, we are represented or misrepre- sented by six councillors,not one of whom resides in the wards ; their residences are where the streets are well Lighted, also, out of the reach of the loose characters, who habitually infest this "lane," and where their wives and daughters are free from the insulting and sometimes brutal importunities of men i various stages of intoxi- cation, and their delicate ears are not offended by the vile and filthy language indulged in by the misguided young women who prowl this road at all hours, from darkness setting in, until daylight appears, end for whom our wives and daughters are often mistaken in the darkness, to which we are evidently condemned, by the incapacity or indifference of those whom we sent to the Council, to quote the ttock expres- sion, to devote their time and attention to the interests of the Ward. Have they dsne so? I think not. This lighting question is no new thing sprung upon them, as it has been going on for years, and so has the iusani:ary condition of our streets, the play-ground of our work- = n's children. We have no Palmyra Squares or Victoria Parks up this direction, although there might be. As the two Wards in question are absolutely working class, this may in a way account for some of the above evils, and in all probabbiry the political club nominees who represent us consider things good enough for us. How much longer the workingmen of these wards are wing to tolerate club management of their local business is a difficult thing for me to determine. But, I think, when the electors begin to weigh performances against speeches, airsi discover the balance in favour of speeches, then, and not until then, shall we begin to consider, like other less important towns, than this one, the advisability of sending workingmen to our Council to represent workingmen, instead of men whose sole desire it is to gain for themselves, a social position, which otherwise, their limited accomplistments are unequal to. As an illustration of how we are represented in this ward; one of our msst gifted councillors at the last meeting of the Couocil, seconded the resolution, for the repaving of Nspier-streer, with wood blocks, at a cost of about 12, 61 per square yard, while at least, one half of hie own ward is without even granite sets, always in a condition nf darkness and greatly in need of sanitary attendon &c. He bad not even a word to say in support of the Councillor, who endeavoured to introduce the l'gSting scandal, but, of course they bdonged to opposite political clubs. Workingmen, how much lsnger will you allow those people to humbug and hoodwink, you, out of your municipal rights ? Again thanking you for your kindness in publishing my last letter, and hoping that ydu will grant the same privilege to the present nip. —I am yours respectfully, MAR TIN FLANAGAN, 151, Orford Lane. Warrington. 18th July, 1900.

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

An important change comes into operation next Wedresday when the sth and 6th battalion i Liver- pool Regiment with headquarters at Warrington become indep-indent units instead of being as they have for many years pas; double battalion militia corps. Prior to the introduction of the territorial sybtem in 1881 it was the old 2nd Royal Lancashire Militia (Duke of Lan- caster's Own Rifles) with headquarters first at Liverpo :I and afterwards at. Warrington. In 1881 the corps became the 3rd and 4th Batta- lions Liverpool Regiment and a few months ago the numerical designation was changed to sth and 6th battalions in coestquence of the formation of 3rd and 4th regular battalions iu conneclon with the. Liverpool Regiment. Now these two militia battalions will be perfectly independent of each other but will still have their headquariers at War- rington and each battalion will consist of eight companies.

Colonel Woodward, the Lkutenant-Uolonel Corn- mandant of the sth and 6th Battalions Liverpool Regiment. will in tuture command only the 6th Battalion hut will retain his rank as Lieutenant Colonel Commandant, while Colonel J. N. Batten the second Li,utenant-Colonel of the corps com- mends the sth Battalion. Major and H in. Lieu- tenant Co.onel Hand will act as second in commano of the 6th Battalion and Major Terry second in com- mand of the sth Battalion.

Secon.i Lieutenant Barry Siell just appointed to the 3rd Battalion south Lancashire Legiment, will, it is unden-tood, do duty tor the present with the depo:, at Warrington. Lieutenant Malcolm-Green, 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, has been promoted Captain in the regiment and takes over cominand of a company in the 2nd battalion of the regiment succeeding Cap- tain Dudgeon appointed to the staff in India. Cap- tain Malcolm-Green was appointed second Lieuten- ant in the Smith Lancashire Regiment in December 1891,and was promAed Lieutenant in August 1894. Major Fraser on promotion to his present rank has been appointed second in command of the 2nd Lancashire Engineer Volunteers at St. Helens. Second Lieut. Dean of the 3rd battalion and second Lieut. Finegan, of the 4th battalion have been promoted to the rank of Lieut. in the Liver- pool It-girnent,

- Captain and Quartermaster Pollitt, who was for several years Q tartermaster of the Ist Battalion Liverpool Regttneqt, has been appointed Q uarter- masttr of the 2nd battalion Royal Lancashire Reserve Regiment. Mr C. Anders has become Quartermaster of the 2nd Lancashire Rugineer Volunteers at St. Helens in succession to Quartermaster Quarmby, wno resigned that appointment a few weeks ago, alter holding it only since last August.

The Warrington-Runcorn Tramway Scheme. The procnot-rs of the scheme for a light railway between Warrington and Runcorn, worked by elec- tricity, nave withdrawn their application to the Board of ''rade for the necessary powers. Railway Servants' Demonstration.

A dem:ei-tration in connection with the local branch of the Amalgamated Society ot Railway Servants took place on Sunday. A procession started frAn the Town Hall about two o'clock, and, headed by the Borough Brass Band,who gen-2rously gave their services, proceeded along Sankev-street, Bridge street, Mersey-street,Fenuell-street.Batt era- .trforii-lane and canners'-lane to 6t, Paul's Church, where a special service was held and a sermon preached by the Rev. EH Tarbuck, vicar, from the words "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this to visit th e fatherless and widows in their affliction and to keep himself uespotted from the world," General Epistle St James i. 27. The preacher said 11,, was aaxious that the great railway workers of the nation should not have their Sundays taken from them in larger proportion every year. He did not altogether blame the masters, as it was natural that in the stress of competilon they should desire to present a decent balance sheet to the stiarrhotilets,but he did to a great extent blame those who employed railway men on the Sunday, There would be no trips advertised if there were no trippers, and, of course, they knew that as de- mand created the supply so the supply created the demand. If these advertisements constantly appeared they would all have visilns of green fields and the seaside on the ~..4unday. and perhaps be ovettempted: He viewed with the most anxious concern the growth of Sunday traffic amongst pas- sengers on the railways of England, Ireland, Scot- land,and Wales. A proportion of them were bound to work. Luggage must go forward, or men would be out of work during the week, but wow' every encouragement was given to people to employ their fellow-workingmen on the Sunday they should put their hands down and say: "As far as we can we will strive to raise a more noble and a more unself- ish opinion about the matter." They were also a chariLable society, and in this connection the preacher read extracts from the annual report of the orphan fund of the A.S.R.S. which he considered was an -xceedingly creditable one, and worthy of his congratulations, and his prayers for their future progress. Another procession started from the 'lowa Hail at BiX o'clock, and the members of the society paraded the principal streets of he town, and aft erwaris attended a service held in Friars- green Chapel in Cairo-street.

div.p: Ti OME-AND FORIEGN MISSIONS.
Sale of Work in the Rectory Grounds.

With the commendable object of supporting several Home and ForAga Missions a sale of work and garden We were opened in tne Rectory Grounds last Thursday week. Charming weather pre- vailed with the result that a large number of people visited the grounds during the afternoon and even- ing. The stalls had he-ti attractively arranged in a marquee, and were laden with useful and orna • mental articles and beautiful flowers. There was also a refreshment tent. The names of the stall holders were Me dames WillissJ anus Craik,Cameron Richard Fairclough, John Craik, and Daikin, and Misses Percival, Nellie Wright and Boyle, and the ladies in charge of the refreshment tent were Misses Ethel White, Duncan, Randle- Ford, Thurston, C Willis. Litton, and Nora Fairclough. A host of attractions was pro- vided, including tennis and croquet tournaments, and a bicycle gvmkana, in which there were a large number of comp-titors. The Blue Coat School Band was in attendance and played selec- tions in capital t•tyle. A number of girls gave a Maypole dance with great credit. The opening ceremony was performed by Mrs. Charlton Parr and amongst those present were the Rector (Rev Canon Willis), Revs U W uickenson, A S Cameron, F E Powell, B Percival, EC E Carleton, F E Evans, and. Pollock Hill, Mrs Beamont, Mrs Willis, Mrs R Fairclough, Mrs Atkin, Mrs Carleton, Mrs Willis. Misses White, Miss Pierpoint, Misses rairclough, and Miss Wright. The RECTOR in opening the proceedings, said he hoped they shoien realize at least £lOO by the sale. It seemed a large sum to ask for but he earnestly hoped they would be able to get it. There were four reasons why be appealed to them. The first was that the object was an entirely unselfish one. They were not begging for themselves or for the parish but the sale was in aid of home and foreign missions. The second reason was that the Societies were most deOrving ones. He had the names of ten to which they should be delighted to give LIO each. The home Socie- ties were, the Christian Know edge Society, the National Society, the Additional Curates' Society, the Waifs and Strays Society,the Mersey Mission,and the Nurses' Insti tute in Warrington. The foreign societies were, the Society for the Pr iriagation of the Gospel in Foreign parts, the Calcutta Missionary Associations, the Central Africa and North China Missions. The third reason was that this year they kept the bicentenary of the society for the Propagation of the Goa)), I in foreign parts. They were earnestly begged by the society to make a large contribution, if poreible to their various needs and he trusted they would be able to do a very great deal for that society. The last reason was the condition of China at the present time. He need not enlarge upon it further than to /Ant out that it had been said, he thought most untruly, that it was the missionaries who were the cause of the deaths. It was not the Churchmen and missionaries that the Chinese cared about. They were the mos•I indifferent race in the world to religion. Be had been told that help bad been refused because the people thought it was the missionaries who had been :the cause of the terrible disaster. The Rector, in conclusion, read the following letter which he had received from the Rev. Mackwood Stevens, general secretary to the North China Mission : —" Whilst, as already known, we are mourning those who have passed away through much suffering in the massacre in China, there are parties of our missionaries now in the greatest necessity at Chefoo and elsewhere. We have already responded to their call for help in the preeent absolutely disorganized state of affairs and have considerably overdrawn our account by kind consent of our bankers and shall have to, to a far greater extent as soon as ever, as we hope and pray that our large party shall' be set free from Tientsin. May we beg that all collections, all branch contributions, all usual subscriptions may be paid. in at once and that where possible extra efforts may be made by sermons, church collections, and may we beg that you yourself and personal friends whom you can influence will help the mission now in its hour of great distress. All cheques should be made payable to the North China Diocesan Fund and crossed Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation:Limited, and sent to nis."

Mrs. PARR. in d claring the sale open, said that when Canon and Mrs Willis took so much interest in other people's welf4re it was their duty to do what they could for them. She earnestly hoped that the efforts which were being made would be entirely successful. (Ap- plause.) .
The RECTOR, in thAnhing Mrs Parr for opening the sale,said they were most sincerely grateful to ht.,r for her kindnegs in coming thmre that day. The businees of the day wag then proceeded with.

Fire at Dallam Brewery. A telephone message was received at the Fire Engine Station at noon on Wednesday of an out- break of fire at the Dallam-lane Brewery of Messrs Peter Walker .and Son. The brigade under the charge of Supsrinteadent Turner promptly turned out with th,4 firs engine "Captain," and were at the trew9ty in a very short space of time. The fire had broken out in the roof of the highest cooling room, a spark from a chimney having, it is supposed, ignited an accumulation of malt dust. The roof was blazing on the arrival of the brigade.and owing to the fact of it being about eighty feet from the ground the fire-extinguishing apparatus at the works could not be used. Superintendent Turner tad lengths of hose taken up the steps over the roof of the general building and by a ladder up the out- aide wall, and a plentiful supply of water being easily obtainable the fire was extinguished in practically a few minutes, and what mighr, easily sieve proved a serious conflagration was averted. The damage is slight. During the dinner hour the workmen were engaged in clearing away the debris.

div.head: CHESHIRE ASSIZES.
div.p: CHESHIRE ASSIZES.
Alleged Slander at Runcorn. DAVIES v. EU B.

At the Nisi Pr; 119 Court, before Mr. Justice Grantham Mr. H Baokes appeared for he plaintiff, and Mr. Moss, M.P., for the detendant. This was an action to recover damages for slander alleged to have been uttered by the defendant, Miss Clara Buck. For the plaintiff evi fence was called to show that the was the wife of Mr. Robert 11 Davies, manager Of hl,l rs. Bradley's ahop,Bridee-st Ruecorn' ad lived neat door t the defendant. On the 4'.h April the plaintiff, her husband, and a boy name Tho Mas Wood were h the backyard adj oining defend- ant's. Mr. Davies was removing a greenhouse, respect- ing which there had been some contention betweee the partics.when the defendant began pushing the same with a clothes-prop. He objected t 3 this course, wh,n the defendant called out in a loud tone of VOIC3 " Wnat about that woman you have got living with you? See is not your wife. I know that." The effect of this slander was to cause the breakdown of the plaintiff's healthoini she had to go away for a month.lt was stated by Mr Bankes that a rumour had got about in the neigh- blurhood that the Wainttff and her husband were not married, which was the cause of much unpleasantness. Evidence was now given that the two were married jo Nlvemher 1897. For the defence it was stated that on the occasion in qaestion defendant was playing with a puppy dog in the back yard, throwing sticks for it to fetch, when Mr. Davies arose above the wad in the next yard and began calling her an old woman and an old maid, using adjectival embellish- ments of a decidedly reprot ensive nature. She retorted that she was no older than was his wife," if she was his wife," She denied using tee language complained of. and Mr. Davies also denied that ascribed to him.' The judge put it to the jury to say whether the statement had been made as alleged, or whether it was merely idle words as between an angry man and an angry woman; also, whether. if damages had been sustained, what the amount should be. The jury first of all said they were of opinion the case should not have been brought into court, and that each party ought to pay their own costs. They were advised to confine their finding to facts, but after conferring together for Some time the foreman said there was no likelihood of their agreeing, they being equally divided. His Lordship said he was in a humlnitarian mood that mo -Glee. an 1 would not confine the jury to the hlackhole,bnt discharge them. It would in effect caw() what had been suggested by the jury—that each party should pay its own costs, and he hoped the air wnqi net " ',might up again.

div.head: Late Mrs. Robert Davies.
div.p: The Late Mrs. Robert Davies.

Reference was made in St. Paul's Ohurch,on Sun- day evening, to the late Mrs. Robert Davies, by the Vicar. the Rev E. R. Tarbuck, who explained that the hu,band of that lady was the chief patron of the living. A few days ago a sorrow fell upon him which was, perhaps. the moit irreparable in the world—the death of one's wife with whom one had lived very many years in a union which was so close that Christ called them together one body. Such a lo,s was a tearing of body and soul asunder, and he fell sure that that congregation would offer to Mr. Robert Davies their deenest sympathy ana their most earnest prayers. He was one of those clmoaratively few men of whom they could say with confidence that he had done more by his eximple even than by his eloquent precepts to raite the moral tone of commercial proverity in the town.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, JULY 27. 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, JULY 27. 1900.
HILL CLIFFE AND ITS HISTORY.
An Antiquarian Trip.

There was an interesting gathering at Hill Cliffe on Tuesday, when ia connection with the series of meetings which have been held during the week to celebrate the hi-centenary of the Liverpool Baptists, about sixty gentlemen travelled from Liverpeol to Hill Cliffe to in- spect the ancient chapel. Among those present were th Revs E E Walter,J Green, H Vaughan Thomas, H J Morley, C F Aked, R Lewis, J G West, W Holro:d. and Dr Hawke!. Daring the afternoon the Rev J S Hughes, the pastor of Hill Cdffe Chap-1, very much in- terested the visitors by his explanations and descriptions of the v orious antiquities connected with Hill Chile which hid been preserved. Tea was subsequently prc- aided, after which a public meeting was held in the chapel, at which Dr Hawkee presided. There was a very good attendance. The Chairman said the chapel at Hill Chile had a lunique hist ny, and he would at,lx the pastor, the Rev J S Hughes, to give them a history of it. Tee Pastor paid : I have been asked to give you a glimpse of our heitory, and to act as guide to the anti- quities of the place. I must ask you to remem- ber that a place of w aship has stood on this spot for centuriee. At first it was nothing more than a cottage, and must have been on ground partly occupied by the cellar of the present ceapel house for some sixty years ago when the chapel was rebuilt, a large baptietry in the sheep . of a cistern was discovered while digging for the foundations wnice no one then c necced with the place,. had ever heeler of and te wiih there was no reference. in 'he existing reeeris. That baptistry must have been of considerable antiquity, and points very dietinetly to the tact, that toe earliest worshippers were acsustomed to immerse. Uefortun- ately, instead of having been preserved, the baptistry was left where it was, and is somewhere underneath where we are now met: I arts afraid the hietorie spirit wa not very strong then. Imagine that small lowly meeting house approached from the lane which was scarcely mire than a foot or bridle path surrounded by trees, and you heve a truly retiree spot,a perfect refilee for Christians, who for some reason did not wish to bs too obtrusive in their religious ex .reises, or who desired a haven of refuge hem pe-s Tutors. Its si- u '- don was eminently adapt-d for this perree.e, very near the boundaries of Lancestare and Cheshire, at a safe distanc t from the 011 Roman-read tie L mdon. It would form almost a natural refuge for the faith ii three couni “s, when threatened with the arm of the law. And the fact that it wd;ajiucted on the edge of a common, known as 11 dell& Cemmon, would disarm suspieion, as tee commons were free to all, to enc imp or assemble. Those who .examined the excavations made at the time the old Baptise", was discovered, state tee?: there were alse traces of narrow underground pa,sages, speaking eloquen,ly of what these ancestors of ours had to endure fir righteousness sake. In s,me banks 04 reference I find the place called "High Cliffe." This is a noistske, as it derives its name from the geograpeicel position it occupi.s in the Cleft of two hills or peaks, and is in reality the Hill in the Cleft, and so it was kn iwn a g'nyratien or two agoos even our old tea cups testify Hill Clift• The origin of the place may be described in the language with which Mosheim describes the origin of ths Bap isrs generally—as lost in the remote deoth, of antiquity—of course we have me documentary evidence of any description that goes beyond the period of the Reforma- tion. One of the sorrows of the Nonconformis historian is the paurety of docurrientary evidence Our persecutors succeeded in making hu!e gaps in our history, and we can otey fo m conjectures, trace cir- cumstannes and make a discriminating use of tr.dition Crosby, the Baptist Historian, m ekes no mention re: Hill Cliffe ; Isinicy c onfessee that he could have nc reliable accounts whatever, in fact, no r 'cords of the Baptists in Lane !shire, Yorkshire and Cheshire. Ie the Beefiet handbook there appears from year to year a brief sum- mary of Baptist history, as introductory te Baetiet authors from 1527-1800 from which Hill Cliff is pereist ently omitted. Although I have called the eu'h oras attention twice to .the omission, and he wrote to me in 1896 saying:—" My lists of Baptist authors did not teed me to cell attention to Hill Chits, theueh the early date should have been named !" hut rh at taam;nl, has nor, appeared yet, and the Baptist hendb ook of teis year 1900 records no church in Live,unol as tiny prior to 1800. Yet Baptists in Livprnool have hail a continuoas history since July 25th. 1700. All this snows how shamefully glectful we are f our history arm just- flee:the agitation which is matte if our denominational papers, for the formation of a Baptist Historical Society The most moderate theory of our origin is that given be a local historian an I antiquarian of 89tril repute, M.. Beamont, who cannot be said to b strongly predisp us d in our favour, states that he believes the church to b the result of till lab mrs of R Teter Holland, who seff .1 tee glary of martyrdom on Sin.thfiel 1, Lendon,in 1558 This n able martyr was a Cheshire man, an ancestor of ' Lord Knutsford, and it ia net et all improbable that he was connected with this, church, seeing that he spent much of his time in this neighbourhood and Wigan.-nd I that two of the name of Holland appear on the earliest, document extant, a letter ant by this church to the , church at Hexham. We believe the church existed before the days of Roger Rolland, but the suggestion that he was the founder, is not unreasonable, as even then it would prove that a work of grace was being maintained here prior to his idustriuons death. Indirect proof is sometimes the strongest proof, and we have a proof of that lencl which practically settles the early origin of this church. In trans-erring som. Property in the immediate neiebbourhood from tne Atley te the Appleton Hall estate some years ago, a d .cumsnt came to light, on which appeared the name of J len Warburton, minister of Hill Cliffe. Now this J ibn Warburton was the sle.oed 4on of Sir John Warburton, of Arley, and he died in 1594. As the Probate Court of , Ch ster peeves, the att-nto of the Rev. A. B. Ken- worthy was called by the estate agent to this, awl that Is how and why we place John Warburton as the first minister of Hill Cliffe..l have tried to trace !he history of this John Warburton in thF2Arley family, but being the second son, and not the !Mr to the estate, his line is not given in beaks on Ceeehire families, and doubtless the fact that his religions views were differ'-n' from the oth, r memters of the family, who were either Catholics or teeloneed to the Established Church, will aceiteint for the silence respecting him, This much we know that he was a soldie-, lived Tit Betionefield,, directly opposite to the right of this chapel, and that be was minister of the Cliffs: These two men take us far back, viz., more than 300 years ago. But my own strong convic- tion is that amongst the earliest worshippers at Hill Cliff° were the Lellanls of the 14th cmturv. There are some who assert that it was Wycliffe's Biti'° men who gave birth to the Lollerds, and that the name was given to them in contempt, as so mane ape. nam have been given to the people of God in their progress through time, the term coming from the high Dutch words' Lullen " to sine—and was given to them be- cause they sane at funerals and other occasiens. But, it is evident., that the Lo lards were in existence some time before Wycliffe made his appearance, an 4 so it Seems far more natural to regard them as the followers or Walter Lollard, a man of enlightened views, inflaxible conrae,e and impassioned eloquence will visited tets country in the early part of the 14. h century and ma acquired great influence and power Coming to the Punts? age we tread on more solid ground, though the evidence is still mainly tradition4l, withith s importan.:difference that local history comes to our aid. During the trouble of the Civil War and Rove- hation, Warrinron was the scene of many conflicts. In 1640 the Earl of D vby, with his forces entrenched him- self in the town, and Sri fierce was the conflict that the ordinary laws of warfare were ignored, and we read that the Royalists killed a godly man and his wife in their own house. These tail are by the cammon consent local traditions. , I even venture to think that it is not at all improbable that a community of Christians met here before the days of the Lollarde: Our distinctive ordinance was known in Cheshire, in the fifth century, when two centinental bishops came over. to Counteract the pernicious teach ing of infant baptism and baptised a large number in , the rive, Allen,nea,r Chester. Toe scene of that baptism is net 20 miles from Hill Chafe. Then in the year 600, the devout monks and christians of Bangor and Isycoed. Flintshire, to the number of 2,000, suffered martyrdom fiir refusing to leapt ZS infants at the bid ding of the Pope. The scene of that massacre is scarcely 30 miles from Hill Chile, and what is mere reasonable than to suopose that some of the Christians of that period &cape% retired to a more secluded part of the country where they and their descendants, quietly nourished their beliefs and privately met for worship, and Hill Chile would present an ideal retreat for such being jest close to the estuary of the Merely. And etice a congregation could meet hare for generations, without calling forth the special attention of the authorities. That Baptiste existed in this country in the early part of the 15th and 16th centuries can be abundantly demonstrated. In the registrar of Gray, Bishop of Ely in 1457 there is a direct reference to a Baptist Church, then exis'ine, and atmet which the Bishop ist comptaininic— in Cheste,ton, Cambridgeshire. That church is now extinct. Hence the church at Bill Cliffs takes at least the next p'ane, and from the standpoint or the longest contintrd history claims to he the oldeTt Baptist and oldsgt Nonconformist Church in the British Isles. I may here remark that a large number of the old grave ecrities have been underground for a considerable number of years. It app'ars that they w .re laid flat, and a pit ce of nigh ground required levelling; it was dne with the result that many of the older stones are buried two and three feet deep. There were none who thought t worth while to preserve them. If I am spared,and have the happy lot of being entrusted with • few pounds for the purpose, I should like to explore mere thoroughly that part of our graveyard,in the hope of finding further confirmations of its antiquity. Several relics have been discovered. One of our present members when helping his father-in-law yearc ago came upon a Wellington b-.ot—of an old kind—with a spur on it in a fair state of preservation. It was supposed to belong to a soldier buried in CtOMWeli'd day,and it was reverently returned to the earth. The same member was present about the same thne,when one of the most ancient of the

gravestones was discovered dewn in the soil into which it had sank, and the date 1523 was not only clear on the etone, but, impressed on the soil most distinctly. A, there was a local dispute then proceeding respecting the claims of Hill Ciiffe to antiquity they felt they laid made a discovery and so lifted it out. Hill Cliffe 13 all the richer for having Cromwell's personality linked witn it, even though only by a passane visit. Allusion was here made to the different ministers .and in bringing his review to a close M Buries said, I have to apologise for having tried your p 'deuce is, long. I found it difficult to compress, and my imag nary excursions have had to be abandoned. 0 wine' re the pressure of historic facts one only can I give. Is is a dream. One Sanday morning I awoke with an instinctive c mvieti net something wend arful had happened, and when I reached Red Lane Bridge, I saw that Hill Cliffs ha i uedergene a marvellous ta-ansforinai tion in the night Instead of these modest baildinga I saw a stately structure, in in dern style with a dash ef ancient Greece about i, and rising from its southern aspect was a tower of magnifi3ent proportions, in upper part of which was a ciock, the fingers of which were! pointing to the hour of ten ; it was a landmark night and day. Tile front facedthe lane and was approacfled by means of steps, on ascending which you passed into a portico upheld.by six massive colurnas. Eirering toe sanctuary, I was entranced by the view for jast before me at the other end I saw three alcoves, sp acions anti beatitilhol in design In the nentral one was the Baptiser, a work of art, in white marble, on eacto si le arid in the centre were doors for toe retirane rooms. 0 the alcove on the right side was ti C immunien Table with th 6 silver vessels set for Comrnetdoe, whilst in the alcove on the left was a maga/elle ntly buet and sweetly toned pipe organ. On the right of the central aiceve was the pulpitoon,picueus to every eye. Turning saw the whole chapel with its spacious seats, lofty elieg, graceful arches; granite pillars, traceried Wirl i9wi, was will propertioaed aed et perfect desiee. Over the Arches were inscribel the names of the Heroes ef the Church and there were three nerneriel gend i et 4. On one I saw the stalwart form of Cromwell, on another saw R eeer Flella wiGh trim flames of itnithfi •Id making his form celestial, a ad on the other the nairelees martyrs of Warrington. I bowed my head and thanker! the Giver of ' all good. It was a sanctuary werthe of the place and the history—a veritable Baptist Cathedral. My own i bed at last. In my ecscac.v I walk, I out to clot. my exeited brain, and wended my way into the graveyard, and there also the mystic change had trans- formed the scene, it was so well ordered, so rich in flowers 'aid foliage, that it remind ad me of the Garden of the Seeolchre. But what delighted me more than anything on the snot where lie the remains of Enenez,r F thim, instead of' the broke(' s one which now raaflrs the glee., I saw a nnbl,, 02111Uarfit in polished eranite,and eh happy , !it wa, 10 tee berm or a pulpit, just ths kind of meaumeet that he would rl sir, will license I his ho 131 for the preaee ing of the vsnel. I ascended that pulpit that night and preached weti enoagh to wake the dead around me— parion the egotism—for alas it was hut a dream. A of dream ' New Chile for the new century hut a which consecration. den Imi/3w-ilea( loyalty. th devout son's and the march of progress may fulfil Boxier than we dare tie think.. (Apolauie )

_ Mr Jam,s K mworthy who has written a history of Hill Cliffe Baptist Church. gave slxn, interesting de-Ails re ptc;inz the place. Toe old chapel he pointed out, would seat 80 people. The preacher based his sermon on the words " And herein is that saying true, one soweth and another reapeth. I sent you to reap that where4n ye bestowed no labour; other men laboured and ye are entered into their labours." lie showed how this generation had entered i ito the labours of others as regarded science, lit irature, the building up of a nation and of the Church.
