div.head: Rev. John Yonge and the Christian Endeavour Convention.
div.p: The Rev. John Yonge and the Christian Endeavour Convention.

The Ross John Yonee prsached a spesial service at Wycliffe Cnurch on Sunday laveniisg on" The Christian Eadeavour Convention just held in London." He observed that no religious occurrence, at least in this country had so powerfully struck the eeneral attention as this Cnristian Eldeavour C invention. Whatever misgiving and lack of sympathy might have existed in some minds concerning the movement the conviction must now be arising thst it was more than justifying itself and aleo thst it had in it possibilities of good far in eX0334 of any of those sinister possibilities that somd might have imagined. It was a saying of the world that " nothing succeeds like suc- cess," and if almost miraculous rapidity of growth, almost wosid-wide acceptance, arousal of an enthusiasm wnicn not (illy failed to evaporate but coo - tinned to increase, and the enlistment in forms of Christian service of millions of young Christian disciples these things were features of success then the Christian Endeavour movement could only be truthfully spoken if 43 one of the very greatest Christian successes I of modern days. One of the most effective styles of teaching in these days was the method of the " obj Ct lesson." This Coristaan E ideavour week in the great metropolis of the British Empire had been the most iin- pressive and cenvincing onject lessoe ot the vitalit7,the luxuriant growth, the splendid fruitfulness, the illimi•- able power of this " Christian Endeavour." A convenciou drawn together from all q srler3 of the globe, and numbering, it was sail, some 40.000 p-rsons was a significant event. It had taken two years of work to complete the arrangements and the financial Cost had been large. London had had mans, monster assemblies, both political and secial, hot this meeting of young people of the Christian Endeavour Societies had surpassed:them all. That fact alone com- pelled the most thoughtful attention to the movement itself. But that attention became rivetted, when it was remembered what this Convention was and from whence it sprang. Little more than 20 years ago, this movement . had in) ex.sience. For thernselves,as Coneregati .nalists the fact should have peculiar interest that Christian Endeavour was the child of a Congregational house, that it held its first meeting in the study of a Congre- gational minister, and had from then until now, Wen presided over, inspired, developed, by the large hearted, unselfish, and unwearied devotion of a Congregational minister. It was one of the misfit re- m irkable shines and one of the divinest marks about the Cnristian Endea your movement that it thus found its origin in an obscure place, and among a handful of ordinary young folk led by a pastor who bad never be ll heard of before. Three things had tended to prejudice the movement with not a few, first, it had given the supreme place to the devotional life, by insisting on the weekly gathering for prayer and testimony ; second, it hail mode this taking of the Christian Endeavour Pledge an essential to membership ; and third, it had been thought to lead young people to care more for Christian Endeavour meetings than for the ordinary meetings of the church or the school. The first two of these things were fundamental and inseparable essentials of the Christian Endeavour Scheme. The pledge was objocted to not so much for what it said as for the fact tnat it was a :pledge. People did not like to be tied down—they did not like to commit themselves to any definite line. lhere were young men who thou 'ht it beneath their dignity to take a Christian pledge. They thought they could be Christians without it, which no one would deny. But if they wanted to join the army and extend or defend the Empire of the Qireen they had to take the oath which was the same thing as taking the pledge. Why should not young ChtigtiAos be as will- ing to take a pledge of service tot the Bing of Kings as for the Queen of England ? The reasons justifying the

pledge were many and that large numbers found it no impediment was clear from the yearly added thousands of th- Universal Eideavour roll. As regarded the third ,bjection he would only say one word and it was this : —chit if Christian Endeavour meetings diverted youn4 people from ordia try e-t tbliehe i church meet- ngs. then such ordinary me tin4s had bAter be revised and remodelled to make th in more attrac- tive. The eiders of the church must Ivep step, if they could with the juniors for the day was past when the young folks would enj slow marches with the old• 9pesking tor himself be did not think it absolutely n:cessary that bAn meetings should be attended. He did not think young people could bs al ,vays attending religious meetings ani if the Christian Endeavour suited ,neu better than the old-fashuned churcn meeting le• ilvm have it and let the eld-rs who could not apprec-- ate the newer style in tics the test and most they could of the fashion they were sceuce•omed to.

Further large profits are anticipated from the acquirement of the Boratera, in connection with the mono-railway. Before asking the public to subscribe the neeessery capital, it' was considered advisable not only to acquire the property, and get everything into actual working order, but to wait until all the necessary concessions had been definitely granted, and deliveries of the borate into this country had actually been commenced. A large calainer has been erected, together with store house ma lager's house, laboratory, bl4cksatith's and joiner's shops, cottages, and a horse and mule corral at Cbilcaya. The company has its own brick field and stone quarry, and a village has been establi hed in the vicinity. A line has already been laid down to take the borate from the deposit to the caleL,er with an embankment of over half- a-mile in length, and stations for which the Government concessions have been obtained, have been established every 16 miles along the whole line t f route to the port.
